notes.note: The arithmetic that can be checked mostly holds: the 28 Aug row reproduces to the cent from C1 ($25.90 → $26 Opus, $10.37 → $10 Sonnet), the $64–160 four-round figure is exactly 4 × the $16–40 column, the 1.9× understatement is 1,597,426 / 833,142 = 1.917, the 1.6–3.1M / median 1.8M range matches C1, the $30–90 room is 6 × $5–15, and the Anthropic $13 / $150–250 / 90%-under-$30 figures are verbatim correct against the cited doc, as are Claude Pro $20/$17, ChatGPT Go $8 and Codex-on-free. The weakness is not in the sums but in the sentences wrapped around them: an average is relabelled a ceiling, a ceiling is contradicted by the page's own next sentence, cache reads that make up over half the price are described as sitting on top of it, and the table's dollar columns cannot be reproduced from the one token column shown — on the page that ends by telling readers a number without a receipt is only a claim.

The arithmetic on this page is unusually clean — I reproduced the 28 Aug row exactly from the project's own token log ($25.91→$26 at $5/$25, $10.36→$10 at $2/$10), the 1.9× understatement, and the $64–160 four-round ceiling. The page is also genuinely honest where it is weakest: it volunteers that the token log is unpublished, that the teaching-session numbers are estimates, and that nothing re-checks itself. The weakness is elsewhere: the most quantitatively specific claims on the page — the $13/day heavy-use figures, the $5/$25 and $2/$10 rates the whole worked example rests on, the $50 allocation, the $100 student credits, the token-ranking anecdote — are attributed to unnamed pages, unnamed coverage, and unnamed organizations, while the three links the page does carry are for the least load-bearing rows. And in one place the footer's blanket "were checked" certifies a claim the project's own notes explicitly mark as the least verified thing they found.

The page's measured spine is sound — I reproduced the 28 Aug run's dollar figures to the cent from the token split in OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1, and the five-run range, median and the 1.9× correction all agree with their sources. What fails is the connective tissue: figures are re-characterised as they travel down the page (an average becomes a ceiling, $6–$40 becomes "single dollars", a four-round cap is disproved in its own paragraph), and "ceiling" and "the one thing that costs" each carry meanings the page elsewhere denies them. The most consequential single defect is line 487's blanket "students excluded", which contradicts both the page's own classroom pricing and points.md §F, and lands on precisely the reader deciding whether to assign this.

The page's honesty apparatus is its best feature and its worst liability: it holds every claim to a receipts standard that its own centrepiece does not meet. Its strongest section — the five-run worked example — is unreconcilable by any reader (no I/O split, no per-run cache column, and a $/token rate that swings 2× across rows with no explanation), and its single most memorable line, "the receipt is on the usage screen," disqualifies the very numbers it is printed next to. The three genuinely blocking items are arithmetic and logic, not tone: cache reads are described as sitting "on top of" dollar figures that already contain them, an enterprise *average* is relabelled a *ceiling*, and "you can complete every step of Cold Start without paying anyone" is false against Cold Start's own default (4.5 creates a private repo; GitHub Free will not serve Pages from one).

The prose is unusually good for its genre: it is specific, it refuses to console, and its best sentences do real work rather than sound well. The best line in the document is line 473, "The cheap prompt and the good prompt are the same prompt" — it turns a money anxiety into a craft instruction in eight words and must survive every edit (runners-up: line 390's "A month is just however many of those you did", and line 484's "They are doing a different, shorter thing, and they will conclude they are bad at it"). The weakest thing is the back half of the provenance apparatus: two captions and a footer paragraph that say the same four caveats three times each, plus a maintainer's voice that keeps leaking into a student handout ("still owed", "a handoff has gone to that project"). And one darling — "the ceiling for one document is four rounds" — is contradicted by the sentence directly after it, which is the one place the page misleads on money.

The arithmetic is right and I could not break it: I reproduced the 28 Aug row to the cent from the source token log in OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1 ($25.90 → $26; $10.36 → $10), and the cited rates ($5/$25 Opus 5, $2/$10 Sonnet 5, cache reads at a tenth) match Anthropic's published list. The plan-versus-meter frame is the best thing on the page and is technically real. The weakness is that the prose repeatedly contradicts the numbers underneath it: a column labelled "Billable tokens" omits the tokens that supply half the bill, a stated "ceiling" is disproved two sentences later, "an eleventh as much" is arithmetically impossible, and the single biggest lever on the bill — output tokens, at 5× input — is absent from the list of levers.

The page is a genuinely good extraction of `points.md` §F and `course-outline.md` §10, and its arithmetic checks out (28 Aug run: 1,359,900 in × $5/M + 236,512 out × $25/M + 26,384,348 cache × $0.50/M = $25.90 → the $26 printed; Sonnet column is exactly 2.5× throughout; 1,597,426 ÷ 833,142 = 1.92, so "1.9× too low" is right). The weakness is systematic and one-directional: where a repo source carries a ⚠ or a hedge beside a fact, the handout keeps the fact and leaves the hedge behind — the "floor" caveat on the five-run table, the "least verified" flag on sponsored keys, §10's caching caveat, and the pruning window on the token log. Second weakness: it re-derives two lists (cost drivers, the ceiling/meter fork) that `course-outline.md` §10 and `points.md` D2 already state more sharply, and drops the best sentence in each.

Read cold, top to bottom, as a biologist who has never run an agent. The prose voice is excellent and the money argument (three shapes, buy a ceiling) lands without any prior knowledge — that is the page's strength. It falls apart at the worked example: "token" is never defined anywhere on the page even though an entire table is denominated in millions of them, "ceiling" carries four different meanings, "run" and "round" are the same thing under two names, and the headline price ($6–$40 to review a document) is contradicted fifteen lines later by the page itself ($64–160). Findings are in the order I hit them, per my brief; severity is in the field.

Census: ~3,430 words in the body plus a 259-word footer, carried by 2 tables, 4 lists, the three-shape grid, and 6 tinted boxes — and zero diagrams. The page is well broken up; there is no wall of prose here, and the three-shape grid (lines 262–281) is the best thing on it, a real taxonomy shown as a structure and then reused as a column in the pricing table. The weakness is concentrated in three places where an argument that is literally a table has been written as paragraphs: the five-run table withholds the one column (cache reads) that explains its own numbers and then explains it in prose instead; the teaching-session section is a two-column plan-vs-meter comparison rendered as seven paragraphs; and the equity section flattens a four-row eligibility matrix that already exists in `points.md` §F into a sentence. Separately, the five-run caption and the footer are the two densest blocks on the page and are set in the smallest, faintest type — 153 and 187 words of atomic sourced facts as unstructured prose.

The file is mechanically clean where it counts: PASS on encoding (pure us-ascii, zero non-ASCII bytes, no mojibake), PASS on entities (9 distinct, all terminated, no bare ampersands), PASS on tag balance (0 unbalanced elements, empty stack at EOF, no mismatched closes), PASS on CSS braces (59/59, final depth 0), PASS on table column counts (3/3 across all 8 rows of table 1, 4/4 across all 6 of table 2, no colspan, both captions correctly first-child), PASS on dark mode (all 14 colour tokens overridden in both the prefers-color-scheme block and the [data-theme="dark"] block, identical sets, body background explicit, light path correctly guarded with :not([data-theme="light"])), PASS on network (Google Fonts only — the one permitted host — with complete fallback stacks; zero scripts, images, iframes), and the missing doctype/head/body is correct, not a defect: docs/handouts/README.md documents these as artifact sources that get wrapped at publish time. Two FAILs: there is no @media print block at all (grep returns nothing, while sibling four-barriers.html has one), and the heading outline skips a level. The print failure is the one that matters — this is the sheet a nervous faculty member prints for a budget meeting, and for a dark-theme reader it prints as near-white text on white paper.

The macro-spine is sound and better than most cost pages: free floor → the shapes of a bill → prices → levers → equity → act. Reassurance ("You can complete every step of Cold Start without paying anyone", line 222) is correctly front-loaded, and the hardware caveat correctly precedes the free-tier claim it qualifies. The weakness is depth, not sequence: the page nominates its own most valuable sentence — "the number worth carrying around" — and files it at roughly 60% depth behind the scariest figure on the sheet, and the one five-minute action that prevents "the only genuinely bad outcome on this page" is 250 lines from the paragraph that names the danger. The closing action list also serves only one of the page's two audiences.

findings.title: Cache reads are already inside the dollar figures, not "on top"
findings.where: Line 385–386: "Between 10.8 and 36.9 million further tokens were read back out of cache on top of those figures"
findings.problem: They are not on top of the dollar figures — they are the largest single component of them. Recomputing the 28 Aug run from OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1 (output 236,512; new input 1,359,900; cache creation 1,014; cache read 26,384,348) at the page's own rates: input 1.360914M × $5 = $6.80; output 0.236512M × $25 = $5.91; cache read 26.384348M × $0.50 = $13.19. Total $25.90 → the $26 in the table. The cache-read line is 51% of the price. At Sonnet rates: $2.72 + $2.37 + $5.28 = $10.37 → the $10 in the table. An anxious reader — the audience this page names — reads "on top of those figures" and concludes the real bill is meaningfully above $40. It is not; the $40 already contains it.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Those dollar figures already include 10.8–36.9 million tokens read back out of cache at a tenth of the input rate — on the 28 Aug run that cache reading is over half the price, which is why the cost is not proportional to the token count shown."

findings.title: A "ceiling" of four rounds that a recorded run exceeded by 3.5×
findings.where: Lines 399–403: "the ceiling for one document is four rounds — call it $64–160 … One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it."
findings.problem: $64–160 is arithmetically right (4 × the $16–40 Opus column) but it is not a ceiling, and the page falsifies its own word two sentences later. The recorded worst case is fourteen rounds: 14 × $16–40 = $224–560 for one document. That number is never given. On a page whose thesis is that a meter has no natural stopping point, the one measured runaway is the most decision-relevant figure available and it is the only one left unpriced — while the reassuring $64–160 is the number set in bold and carried away.
findings.fix: Drop the word "ceiling": "the process repeats until it converges — four rounds is the intended stop, call it $64–160 at the larger model's rates. One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it: $224–560 for a single document. Nothing was broken. Nobody was watching."

findings.title: An average from the source is restated as a ceiling
findings.where: Line 342: "it is roughly the ceiling of what a single very heavy human being can spend"
findings.problem: The cited source (code.claude.com/docs/en/costs) says "the average cost is around $13 per developer per active day and $150-250 per developer per month, with costs remaining below $30 per active day for 90% of users." Line 338 quotes that correctly, then line 342 converts the average into a ceiling. An average is not a ceiling — and the page's own next clause disproves it: if 90% stay under $30 per active day, a user at that 90th percentile runs roughly $450–630 a month at 15–21 active days, two to three times the "ceiling". The page's own worked example disproves it too: the fourteen-round run above is $224–560 for one document. Told $150–250 is the ceiling, a reader who sees $400 concludes the tool is broken or they are being billed wrongly, when they are simply above the mean.
findings.fix: "The figure is useful for one thing: it is roughly the middle of what a full-time engineer spends. It is an average, not a cap — one in ten exceeds $30 on an active day, and a single runaway task on this page costs more than a month of it. If your bill approaches $150–250 you are working like a full-time engineer; if it passes it, nothing has gone wrong."

findings.title: The five-run table cannot be reproduced from the column it shows
findings.where: Lines 362–363 (caption): "Dollar figures computed from those token counts at published list rates"; table columns at lines 372–379
findings.problem: They are not computed from those token counts. "Billable" is input + output + cache creation; the dollar figures additionally require the output/input split and the per-run cache-read count, neither of which is on the page. Try it as a reader on the 28 Aug row: 1,597,426 tokens priced entirely as input is $7.99; entirely as output is $39.94; at the actual 85/15 split it is $12.71. None of these is $26. Worse, the table is non-monotonic in the only number shown — 24 Aug (1,700,364 tokens) costs $30 while 22 Aug (1,863,469 tokens) costs $26 — so a reader who tries to sanity-check it concludes the table is wrong. The page insists the example is checkable ("You can go and look at the task before you judge the price"), and this is the one part of it that is not.
findings.fix: Add two columns — "Output tokens" and "Cache read" — or at minimum a footnote giving the 28 Aug row's full working ($6.80 input + $5.91 output + $13.19 cache read = $25.90), so one row can be verified end to end and the rest inherit its credibility.

findings.title: The 10.8M cache floor is incompatible with the 17 Aug row
findings.where: Line 376: "17 Aug | 1,786,769 | $16 | $6" against line 385: "Between 10.8 and 36.9 million"
findings.problem: The two money columns are exactly 2.5× apart at every rate ($5/$2, $25/$10, $0.50/$0.20), so both columns constrain the same unknowns. Write cost = 5B + 20·output + 0.5·cache (millions). B = 1.786769, so 5B = $8.93. Rounding bounds the true Opus figure to [15.50, 16.25) — the upper bound comes from the Sonnet column needing to round to $6. So 20·output + 0.5·cache ∈ [6.57, 7.32]. If cache ≥ 10.8M then 0.5·cache ≥ 5.40, forcing output ≤ 95,800 tokens across all eleven agents — 8,709 each, below the smallest single agent's output in the only run we can inspect (14,272 on 28 Aug). Run the same algebra on the other four rows using the 28 Aug output share (14.8%) and they land at 21–34M cache, all comfortably in range; 17 Aug lands at 2.5–4.0M. Either the 17 Aug dollar figures are wrong or the stated minimum is not 10.8M.
findings.fix: Recheck the 17 Aug row against the token log. If its cache reads really are ~3M, the range is roughly 3–37M, not 10.8–36.9M, and the sentence explaining why cost is not proportional to length gets stronger, not weaker.

findings.title: The measured cost excludes the session that ran the review
findings.where: Line 384: "reviewing one document properly costs somewhere between $6 and $40"
findings.problem: OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1 states the figure "counts the eleven reviewers only — the session that spawns them, reads eleven reports and writes the record is not in it, so the number is a floor." The page presents it as the cost of the review. The omitted session is not trivial: it reads eleven reports and writes the record, so it is a twelfth context on top of eleven. A reader budgeting a class or a grant line from $6–40 is budgeting from a number the source explicitly labels incomplete — and this page's own closing argument is that a number an agent reports about itself is a claim, not a receipt.
findings.fix: After the range, add: "That counts the eleven reviewers only. The session that launches them, reads eleven reports and writes the record is not in it, so treat $6–40 as a floor."

findings.title: The $6–40 range silently switches models mid-range
findings.where: Line 384: "between $6 and $40"
findings.problem: $6 is the 17 Aug run priced at Sonnet; $40 is the 14 Aug run priced at Opus. No single model produces that band. Held at one model the ranges are $16–40 (Opus) and $6–16 (Sonnet). A reader plans on "$6–40", picks the larger model because the page has just told them independence is the product, and under-budgets the low end by 2.5×. The caption works hard to say the two columns are the same tokens at two models, then the prose that readers actually carry away collapses them into one span.
findings.fix: "So: reviewing one document properly costs $16–40 on the larger model, or $6–16 on the mid-sized one — the model choice moves the price by 2.5×, and the length of the document moves it about the same again."

findings.title: "An eleventh as much" is asserted with no measurement behind it
findings.where: Lines 395–396: "One agent walking the same eleven checklists costs an eleventh as much"
findings.problem: Nothing measured supports it, and the mechanism argues against it. One agent walking eleven checklists in one context reads the document once but re-sends a context that grows with each checklist, so its cost is not the eleven-agent total divided by eleven. The preceding clause ("Eleven agents cost roughly eleven times one agent") is supported — C1's per-role billable spans 100,369–186,886 against a total of 1,597,426 — but the converse is a different claim. On a page that ends by saying an unmeasured number is a claim and not a receipt, this is the one unmeasured number stated as fact.
findings.fix: Soften to the supported half: "Eleven independent agents cost roughly eleven times one — C1's per-role figures run 100k–187k billable each. One agent walking the same eleven checklists is cheaper, though not by eleven, and it shares a mind with the author, so it agrees with itself."

findings.title: The $50 caveat points at the wrong university page
findings.where: Lines 443–444: "reported as $50 in secondary coverage; the university's own pricing page states no amount"
findings.problem: points.md F attaches the $50 to the Codex for the Classroom stipend and says "the ITS page itself states no amount" — the classroom page, not the pricing page. The pricing page does state amounts: points.md records it publishing claude-opus-5 at $5.00/$25.00 per 1M, claude-sonnet-5 at $2.00/$10.00, claude-haiku-4-5 at $1.00/$5.00. A reader who follows the caveat to the pricing page finds prices there and concludes the caveat is overstated, which undermines the most carefully hedged claim on the page. The body text also flattens "classroom stipend" into "classroom allocation" (line 421), losing that it is a grant-bound figure.
findings.fix: "reported as $50 per user per month in secondary coverage; the classroom page itself states no amount — the university's pricing page publishes per-token rates, not a stipend."

findings.title: Two priced claims cite "the vendor's page" with no link
findings.where: Line 292 (caption): "Read 29 August 2026 from the vendors' own pages — Claude, Codex, Gemini CLI, Dropbox"; rows at lines 318–320 and 328–330
findings.problem: Claude, Codex and Gemini CLI are linked; Dropbox is named in the caption and in the 2 GB / ~$10 claims at line 210 and line 319 with no link anywhere on the page, and the $10–15/yr domain price at lines 214 and 329 has no registrar link at all. Line 226 sets the rule the page then breaks: "Treat the numbers as orders of magnitude and the links as the authority. When this matters, go and look at the vendor's page." A reader told to go and look is given no address for two of the seven table rows.
findings.fix: Link the Dropbox plans page from the storage row and cite one named registrar's renewal price for the domain row, or drop Dropbox from the caption's source list and say plainly that the storage and domain figures are typical market prices rather than readings from a page.

findings.title: Footer certifies as "checked" a claim the source flags as least verified
findings.where: Line 487: "A graduate student employed as a research or teaching assistant can often be sponsored" — and line 541: "The institutional and student-credit facts were checked at one university on 27 August 2026"
findings.problem: points.md §F records this as: "the FAQ indicates faculty may sponsor keys for employed students... ⚠ Single source, read once, not confirmed on a second page. It is the most decision-relevant line found and the least verified." The handout drops every hedge — "the FAQ indicates" becomes a flat assertion, "would cover GSRAs and GSIs" becomes "can often be sponsored" — and then the footer sweeps it into a blanket statement that the institutional facts "were checked." A reader has no way to tell this sentence apart from the four sentences around it that rest on four separate linked pages. This is precisely the defect the project itself names in OPEN-FINDINGS residual 6: "a partial flag reads as a receipt... flagging one silently certifies the rest." The consequence is concrete: a faculty member reads this and tells a GSRA they can be sponsored, on the strength of one FAQ line nobody confirmed.
findings.fix: Carry the source's own flag into the sentence: "a graduate student employed as an RA or TA appears to be sponsorable — this rests on a single FAQ line, read once and not confirmed elsewhere, and it is the least verified fact in this section." Then narrow the footer from "the institutional and student-credit facts were checked" to name which ones were and which one was not.

findings.title: The heavy-use figures name a source but link nothing
findings.where: Line 338: "Anthropic's own cost documentation reports that across enterprise deployments the average is around $13 per developer per active day, and $150–250 per developer per month, with 90% of users staying under $30 on an active day."
findings.problem: Three specific numbers and a percentile, attributed to an entire documentation site rather than a page, with no link. The page's whole point about heavy use — and the flag box at 340–343 that builds an argument on it — rests on figures the reader cannot reach. There is an Anthropic docs link on the page (line 477, code.claude.com/docs/en/costs) but it is introduced 140 lines later as documentation of "the mechanism" for reading your own usage, so nothing tells the reader it is also the source for these numbers. If it is the source, the page has hidden it; if it is not, the source is nowhere. These figures also appear nowhere else in the repository — grep finds them only in this file — so there is no second record to fall back on.
findings.fix: Link the specific page at the point of use: "Anthropic's own cost documentation reports…" — and if that is not where the $13 / $150–250 / 90%-under-$30 figures come from, name and link the page that is.

findings.title: The rates that produce every dollar in the worked example are sourced to "the vendor's page"
findings.where: Lines 366–369: "a larger model at $5 in / $25 out per million tokens and a mid-sized one at $2 in / $10 out, both read from the vendor's page on 29 August 2026"
findings.problem: Every dollar figure in the five-run table, the "$6 and $40" headline at line 384, the "$26 for a review" at line 354 and the "$64–160" ceiling at line 400 are computed from these two rate pairs. The rate pair is the only half of the calculation a reader could actually check today — the footer already concedes the token log "is not yet published." And it is sourced to an unnamed "the vendor's page," with no link, on a page that links claude.com/pricing three sections earlier for subscription plans. So both inputs to the page's most load-bearing number are unreachable, one of them for want of one href. (I confirmed the method reproduces: 1,359,900 new input + 1,014 cache creation at $5/M, 236,512 output at $25/M, 26,384,348 cache reads at $0.50/M = $25.91, the table's $26. A reader deserves the chance to do that themselves.)
findings.fix: Name and link the page the rates were read from, in the caption and again in the footer where the same $5/$25 and $2/$10 are repeated. points.md §F sources them as matching Anthropic list pricing; link claude.com/pricing or the API pricing page directly.

findings.title: $50 allocation sourced to unnamed "secondary coverage," and blamed on the wrong page
findings.where: Lines 443–444: "The per-user monthly allocation is reported as $50 in secondary coverage; the university's own pricing page states no amount."
findings.problem: Two problems in one sentence. First, "secondary coverage" is never identified — not a publication, not a date, not a link — so a reader cannot weigh whether $50 is a trade-press figure, a forum post, or a press release, and the whole $30–90-for-the-room estimate hangs off it. Second, the page identified as silent is the wrong one. points.md §F attaches the warning to the Codex-for-the-Classroom bullet — "the ITS page itself states no amount" — while the university's actual pricing page is cited a few lines earlier as publishing amounts in detail ($5.00/$25.00 per 1M for claude-opus-5, and so on). A reader who follows this instruction goes to the pricing page, finds published rates, and concludes the handout is wrong about the one thing it flagged.
findings.fix: Name the secondary source or say what kind it is ("reported at $50 in trade coverage of the program launch"), and correct which page is silent: it is the classroom-programme page that states no per-user amount, not the pricing page.

findings.title: The $100 student credit programme is described but never named or linked
findings.where: Line 491: "One offering $100 of credits to students, verified against a university email address, is United States and Canada only."
findings.problem: This is the single most actionable eligibility fact on the page for a student reader, and it is written so that they cannot act on it. The programme is unnamed and unlinked, so a student outside the US and Canada cannot confirm they are excluded, and one inside cannot go and claim it. points.md §F has everything needed and it was dropped: the $100 Codex student credits, the link at developers.openai.com/community/students, SheerID verification, 2,500 credits, a 12-month expiry, and the fact that it works on a free ChatGPT account. Anonymising a vendor programme is not the same editorial call as anonymising the university — there is no privacy interest here, only a lost citation.
findings.fix: Name and link it: "OpenAI's $100 Codex student credits, verified by SheerID against a university address and usable on a free ChatGPT account, are United States and Canada only."

findings.title: Table caption claims four sources; the table carries links to two of them
findings.where: Line 292 caption: "Read 29 August 2026 from the vendors' own pages — Claude, Codex, Gemini CLI, Dropbox"
findings.problem: The caption makes an explicit provenance claim for all seven rows and then honours it for three. Dropbox is named as a source and appears nowhere on the page as a link — neither in this table's "from ~$10/mo" row nor at line 210 where the "2 GB" free-tier figure is stated. The heavy-tier row ($100–200/mo, Claude Max and ChatGPT Pro) has no link. The domain row (~$10–15/yr) has no link and no registrar named. And the one link on the free-tier row points at github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli — a source repository, not a pricing page, and not a page that states the free-tier quota the $0 depends on. A caption that says "read from the vendors' own pages" reads as a receipt for the whole table.
findings.fix: Either add the missing links (Dropbox plans, Anthropic and OpenAI plan pages for the heavy tiers, a named registrar for the domain figure, Google's Gemini CLI quota page rather than the repo), or narrow the caption to say which rows are linked and that the rest are order-of-magnitude figures held without a citation.

findings.title: "Some organizations" ranking people by token consumption has no source at all
findings.where: Line 511: "Some organizations have gone as far as ranking people by token consumption"
findings.problem: This is the closing claim of the equity section — the beat the whole argument lands on — and it is an empirical assertion about real organisations with no attribution of any kind: no organisation named, no coverage cited, no date, not even "reported." It appears nowhere else in the repository; grep finds it only in this file. On a page whose own thesis is that "a number an agent gives you about its own consumption is a claim, not a receipt" (line 411), an unsourced claim about other people's numbers is the weakest sentence to end on.
findings.fix: Either cite it — name one organisation or the coverage it comes from — or demote it to a hypothetical the page owns: "Where consumption is visible, it invites being ranked, and a ranking of tokens measures budget and confidence, not work." The argument survives the demotion; the unsourced factual claim does not need to be made.

findings.title: The one verifiable run is dated a day off from the project's own record
findings.where: Line 379: "28 Aug1,597,426"
findings.problem: This is the only row a reader with repository access could actually check, and the label makes it harder to find. docs/cases/OPEN-CORRECTIONS.md §C1 records these exact figures — 1,597,426 billable, 26,384,348 cache read — as "the run of 2026-08-27 21:51 EDT." The handout files it as 28 Aug, presumably in UTC. Anyone matching the table against the correction record looks for a 28 Aug run and finds a 27 Aug one. Given that the footer already concedes the log is unpublished, the date is the only handle a checker has.
findings.fix: State the timezone in the caption ("run dates in UTC") or relabel the row 27 Aug to match the record the figures come from.

findings.title: Two anecdotes carrying the section's moral point nowhere the reader can check
findings.where: Line 401 "One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it" and lines 408–409 "the same review was reported at 833,142 tokens by the agent that ran it, described as measured"
findings.problem: Both are exact and both are attributed to nothing. "One recorded run" — recorded where? "833,142 tokens" is quoted to the digit with no pointer, and it carries the page's stated takeaway ("If you take one thing from this page"). Both are documented in this repository: OPEN-CORRECTIONS §C1 holds the 833,142 story in full, and notes the fourteen-round run is corroborated by a bugarach record carrying rounds: 14. A reader who wants to believe the page's most memorable lesson has nothing to follow. Worth noting too that C1's status is "open, not yet applied," so the case file it corrects still prints 833,142 as fact at line 218 — pointing at C1 rather than the case file matters.
findings.fix: Add a one-clause pointer to each, the way line 352 does for murderboard — e.g. "recorded in this project's own corrections log" with a link, or name the record for the fourteen-round run.

findings.title: Institutional facts checked at a university the page will not name
findings.where: Line 487: "Checked at one large public university in August 2026"
findings.problem: Anonymising the institution is a defensible editorial choice and the footer discloses it ("checked at one university on 27 August 2026 and are generalized here"), so this is not a hidden gap. But the effect on a reader is that four separately-linked, individually-checkable pages in points.md §F — the free chat service, the API gateway, the Claude Code page, the classroom programme — collapse into one assertion nobody outside this project can re-check, on a page whose own banner tells the reader to "go and look at the vendor's page" when it matters. Students taught at that institution are exactly the readers who would benefit from the four URLs.
findings.fix: If the course is taught at that institution, name it and link the four pages, dated. If it must stay anonymous, say why in one clause ("anonymised because the arrangement is specific and will change") so the reader knows the omission is deliberate rather than an unrecorded source.

findings.title: Page says students are excluded from agents, then prices six students on one
findings.where: Line 487: "staff and faculty only, students excluded, sharing prohibited" — against lines 417–423
findings.problem: The equity section states flatly that at the checked university "the agent sits behind an employment check and a departmental billing code — staff and faculty only, students excluded", and line 488 generalises it: "the institution itself draws a line between chat and agent, and it draws it along employment status." Seventy lines earlier the page prices "six students, one ninety-minute session" against "the university['s] classroom allocation per user per month". Both cannot be true. points.md §F resolves it: the table row "Codex for the Classroom | students in a provisioned Canvas course | grant, else your Shortcode | Yes" is a student-accessible agent route, and OPEN-FINDINGS N1 says so explicitly — "The capped case exists only for students under a classroom grant." The "students excluded" line in the source applies to one row only (Claude Code via Toolkit), not to "the agent". A faculty reader deciding whether they can assign this is told no by one section and given a per-student price by another.
findings.fix: Scope the claim to the product it came from: "one vendor's agent sits behind an employment check and a billing code — staff and faculty only. A second route exists for students in a provisioned course, on a grant or the same billing code, and it is the route the classroom figures below assume." Keep the chat-versus-agent point, which survives; drop the blanket "students excluded", which does not.

findings.title: A four-round ceiling stated as fact, disproved in the next sentence
findings.where: Lines 400–403: "the ceiling for one document is four rounds — call it $64–160 … One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it."
findings.problem: The paragraph states a bound and then reports a run that broke it by 3.5×, without ever saying the bound did not hold. A cost-anxious reader carries away $64–160 as the worst case for one document. Fourteen rounds at the same $16–40-per-round band is $224–560. OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1 corroborates the fourteen-round run ("a bugarach record carries rounds: 14") and states the mechanism — "the cap bounds only rounds, and every round re-runs all eleven" — so the fourteen-round run is not an anomaly the reader can discount. As written the page's largest published worst case is one it has already recorded being exceeded.
findings.fix: Either the four-round cap is configuration that was not on for the fourteen-round run — say so, and give both numbers: "$64–160 with the cap set; the one recorded uncapped run went fourteen rounds, which at the same rates is $224–560" — or the cap is aspirational, in which case delete the word "ceiling" and present $64–160 as a typical converged run, not a bound.

findings.title: $150–250/month is called the average, then used as the ceiling
findings.where: Line 338 "the average is around $13 per developer per active day, and $150–250 per developer per month" vs line 342 "it is roughly the ceiling of what a single very heavy human being can spend"
findings.problem: The same figure carries two incompatible meanings four lines apart. An average has half the population above it; a ceiling has none. The flag's reassurance — "If your bill approaches it, you are not being unlucky, you are working like a full-time engineer" — only works if the number is a high percentile, but the sentence that introduced it says it is the mean of the same population. The page cites the 90th-percentile figure ($30 on an active day) in the same sentence, so it has the vocabulary for the distinction and does not use it. A reader who wants to know how bad it can get is given a number that is, by the page's own framing, routinely exceeded.
findings.fix: Pick one reading and hold it. If $150–250 is the reported average, say so in the flag too and add a ceiling only if a percentile figure is available: "that is the average, so plenty of engineers spend more; treat it as the middle of full-time professional use, not the top of it." Do not let "average" in line 338 become "ceiling" in line 342.

findings.title: "Single dollars for a serious one" is credited to a table that says $6–$40
findings.where: Line 429: "At the per-task rates established above — a few cents for a small task, single dollars for a serious one"
findings.problem: What was established above is line 384, "reviewing one document properly costs somewhere between $6 and $40", and line 354's headline "$26 for a review". Neither $26 nor $40 is single dollars. The back-reference "established above" is load-bearing: the whole meter-priced classroom estimate — "six students … plausibly consume a few dollars in total for the whole room" — is derived from it. Line 390 introduces the same slippage first ("a few dollars for a serious piece of work") immediately after the $6–$40 sentence. The result is that the page's most reassuring number for an instructor rests on a per-task rate the page's own measured table contradicts by roughly an order of magnitude.
findings.fix: Say what the measured band actually supports and where the classroom differs: "the measured serious task above is $6–$40, but that is eleven agents on one long document. A beginner's request is a single agent and a short session — cents to low single dollars — which is why six students for ninety minutes plausibly lands in the low tens of dollars at most." Cite the difference explicitly rather than restating $6–$40 as "single dollars".

findings.title: The 17 Aug row and the 10.8M cache floor cannot both be right
findings.where: Line 376 "17 Aug | 1,786,769 | $16 | $6" against line 386 "Between 10.8 and 36.9 million further tokens were read back out of cache"
findings.problem: The 28 Aug row reproduces exactly from OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1 (1,360,914 in + 236,512 out + 26,384,348 cache read, at $5/$25 and a tenth of input: 6.81 + 5.91 + 13.19 = $25.91 → $26; Sonnet 2.72 + 2.37 + 5.28 = $10.36 → $10), which confirms the method. Apply it to 17 Aug: if cache reads were at least 10.8M, cache alone costs $5.40, leaving at most $10.60 for 1,786,769 billable tokens. Even charging all of them at the $5 input rate costs $8.93, so the output premium of $20/M can cover at most ~83,000 output tokens across eleven agents — against the 236,512 that C1 records for the smaller 28 Aug run. Holding the 28 Aug output share (14.8%) constant, 17 Aug implies about 3.6M cache reads, while the other four runs imply 22–33M. The stated floor of 10.8M is not reachable for that row.
findings.fix: Re-derive the cache range from the same log the dollars came from and print it per run rather than as one band, or drop the floor and state only what is on record ("the one run with a published split read 26.4M further tokens out of cache"). If $16 for 17 Aug is correct, the range is wrong; if the range is correct, that row's dollar figure is.

findings.title: Caption gives two incompatible accounts of where the price band comes from
findings.where: Lines 366–369: "the runs were not all on the same model, so the range is a band rather than a price" and "The two money columns are the same tokens priced at two different models"
findings.problem: These explain the same band two different ways. If both columns are the same tokens repriced at two fixed rate cards, then which model each run actually used is irrelevant to the columns — the numbers would be identical either way. The data confirms it: the Sonnet column is exactly 0.4× the Opus column in every row (40→16, 16→6.4, 26→10.4, 30→12, 26→10.4), which is precisely the ratio of $2/$10 to $5/$25. The band is produced entirely by the deliberate repricing and by run size, not by mixed models. The first clause tells a reader the underlying measurement is heterogeneous, which would undermine the table; the second tells them it is uniform, which is what the arithmetic shows.
findings.fix: Delete the first clause. The honest version is one sentence: "the same measured tokens, priced at two rate cards; the band is the spread across five runs, doubled by the choice of model." If the runs genuinely used different models, that is a separate caveat about the token counts and needs stating as one, not as an explanation of the dollar range.

findings.title: "The one thing that costs" heads a section listing three things that cost
findings.where:
Line 258: "

The one thing that costs: the agent

"
findings.problem: The page opens with "Four things in Cold Start can cost money" (line 201) and the table under this heading prices two of the other three — "Synced storage above the free tier … from ~$10/mo" and "A domain name … ~$10–15/yr". The heading is shorthand for the sub-point at line 206 ("the only one where the amount is open-ended") but does not say so, and it directly negates the lede a reader saw 57 lines earlier. This is the same class of defect the git log already records being fixed once ("The cost sheet said the floor was free while the runbook it costs charges for four things").
findings.fix: Make the heading say the thing that is actually true: "The one that is open-ended: the agent". That keeps the emphasis and stops contradicting the lede.

findings.title: "Ceiling" carries four different meanings on a page that polices exactly this
findings.problem: The page defines "a ceiling" at line 264 as Shape 1, a subscription with an allowance that stops you. It then uses the word for: a fixed recurring price with no allowance at all (line 330, a domain name at $10–15/yr — nothing about a domain stops); the top of a spending distribution (line 342); a cap on rounds (line 400); and prepaid capacity, "a ceiling you have bought whether or not you reach it" (line 432). The page shows it knows this is a hazard — the five-run caption stops to say "'Tier' here means the model, not the plan — the plans in the table above are a different thing that unfortunately shares the word" — and then does the same thing with its own headline term.
findings.fix: Reserve "Ceiling" in the Shape column for things that stop. Label the domain and storage rows "Fixed" or "Flat fee". At line 342 use "the top end" and at line 400 use "the cap", leaving "ceiling" to mean one thing.

findings.title: Three shapes are defined, then the table collapses two of them into one row
findings.where: Line 323: "Per-token, on a card or a billing code" — Shape column "Meter"
findings.problem: Lines 269–280 spend two panels arguing that a personal meter and an institutional billing code are different shapes with different worst cases ("a number you did not agree to" versus "a conversation with your head of department"), and line 222 promises "there are three". The table then merges them into a single row with a single label, and the Shape column never contains the third value. A reader scanning the table for the taxonomy they were just taught finds only two of the three shapes in it.
findings.fix: Split the row, or label it "Meter (yours or theirs)" and add a half-line pointing back to the distinction. The cheapest fix is two rows: "Per-token, on your card — Meter" and "Per-token, on a billing code — Someone else's meter".

findings.title: Row dated 28 Aug is dated 27 Aug in the source the footer says to check it against
findings.problem: OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1 attributes 1,597,426 to "the run of 2026-08-27 21:51 EDT". The footer's whole defence of this table is checkability against that log — "summed per run on 29 August 2026 … the table is checkable only by someone with the file." A checker matching rows by date finds no 28 Aug run. The likely cause is a UTC rendering of a 21:51 EDT timestamp, which is a fine reason and an invisible one.
findings.fix: Label the rows in the same timezone as the log, or add "(local dates; the 28 Aug row is the run of 27 Aug 21:51 EDT)" to the caption.

findings.title: A bolded absolute about the free floor rests on two hedged conditions
findings.where: Line 222: "You can complete every step of Cold Start without paying anyone"
findings.problem: The two cost items this depends on are both hedged twenty lines above: the review folder "usually fits" in a 2 GB free tier (line 210), and research storage is something "most people need neither" of (line 217). "Usually" and "most people" do not add up to "every step", stated in bold with no qualifier. This is the page's own hedge-consistency rule applied to its most reassuring sentence: the same fact is conditional in one place and absolute in another, and the absolute version is the one set in bold.
findings.fix: Carry the condition into the claim: "Most people can complete every step of Cold Start without paying anyone — on free tiers, with no domain, provided the review folder stays inside a free storage tier and you do not need research storage." One clause, and the two hedges above stop being contradicted.

findings.title: "Without paying anyone" is false against Cold Start's own default
findings.where: Line 222: "You can complete every step of Cold Start without paying anyone"; line 244: "Nothing in Cold Start needs a paid tier."; line 252 GitHub Pages bullet
findings.problem: Cold Start 4.5 hands the learner `gh repo create first-project --private --source=. --push` (cold-start.html:756) and Phase 7.4 then says "repository → Settings → Pages → Custom domain" (cold-start.html:960-965). GitHub's own docs: "If the account that owns the repository uses GitHub Free or GitHub Free for organizations, the repository must be public." Pages from a private repo requires GitHub Pro. So the default path this course walks a reader down hits a paywall at Phase 7, on the exact page whose job is to promise it will not. The page compounds it by asserting "unlimited repositories — public or private" and "GitHub Pages... serve a site for nothing" three lines apart, so the reader assembles the false combination from two individually true statements. This is the most embarrassing item here: a check that could have failed, on the page's own headline claim, and nobody ran it.
findings.fix: Either add to the Pages bullet: "On the free plan, Pages serves only from a public repository — Cold Start 4.5 creates a private one, so either make it public before Phase 7 or serve from Cloudflare Pages, which does publish from a private repo for free." Or change Cold Start 4.5's default. Do not leave line 222 as an unqualified promise.

findings.title: Cache reads are inside the dollar figures, not "on top of" them
findings.where: Lines 384-386: "costs somewhere between $6 and $40. Between 10.8 and 36.9 million further tokens were read back out of cache on top of those figures"
findings.problem: The nearest antecedent of "those figures" is the $6–$40 range in the preceding clause, so the sentence tells the reader the cache reads are an uncounted extra. They are not — the caption (line 366-369) says cache reads are priced at a tenth of input, and they dominate. Recomputing the 28 Aug run from its logged split (output 236,512; new input 1,359,900; cache read 26,384,348 — OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1) at Opus-5 rates: $6.80 input + $5.91 output + $13.19 cache = $25.90, which is the table's $26. The cache reads are 51% of that number, already in it. A reader who believes line 385 concludes the real cost of a review exceeds $40; a reader who tries to budget adds a phantom second charge. Either way the page's own headline number is destroyed by the sentence immediately after it.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "Those dollar figures already include 10.8–36.9 million cache reads per run, billed at a tenth of the input rate — on the 28 Aug run that was $13 of the $26, which is why cost does not track the token column."

findings.title: An enterprise average is relabelled as a ceiling
findings.where: Line 342: "it is roughly the ceiling of what a single very heavy human being can spend" (referring to line 338's "$150–250 per developer per month")
findings.problem: I fetched the source. Anthropic's cost docs say verbatim: "the average cost is around $13 per developer per active day and $150-250 per developer per month, with costs remaining below $30 per active day for 90% of users." The quotation on line 338 is accurate; the gloss on line 342 is not. An average is not a ceiling — by construction a large share of that population spends more. The page's own quoted 90th-percentile figure proves it: if 10% of users exceed $30 on an active day, then at ~20 active days those users are above $600/month, 2.4–4× the number the reader has just been told is the ceiling. The anxious department head this page is written for takes $250/month away as the worst case and is wrong by a factor of at least two. This is the page's single most consequential sentence for a budgeting decision and it is a misreading of a statistic printed four lines above it.
findings.fix: Replace with: "That is an average, not a cap — the same document says 10% of users exceed $30 on an active day, which is north of $600 a month. Read it as: if your bill is in this range you are working like a full-time engineer, and there is no ceiling above it except one you set."

findings.title: The "eleven times / an eleventh" claim is the exact defect the page exists to warn about
findings.where: Lines 394-398: "Eleven agents cost roughly eleven times one agent... One agent walking the same eleven checklists costs an eleventh as much"
findings.problem: Two paragraphs later the page delivers its best line — "a number an agent gives you about its own consumption is a claim, not a receipt" (line 411-412) — and records that the last such claim was 1.9× wrong. Yet the 11× / 1/11 counterfactual has no measurement anywhere: there is no single-agent row in the table, no single-agent run in murderboard's log, and no arithmetic shown. It is also almost certainly wrong in the stated direction. One agent walking eleven checklists in one conversation accumulates context across all eleven, so its input grows superlinearly, while eleven parallel agents share a cached prefix — the 28 Aug run shows 26.4M cache reads against 1.36M new input, i.e. 95% of input served at a tenth price precisely because eleven readers hit the same prefix. The page's own data suggests the sequential single agent is nowhere near 1/11, and may not be cheaper at all. Asserting it flatly, in bold, on this page, is self-refuting.
findings.fix: Either measure it — one single-agent eleven-checklist run, added as a sixth row — or downgrade to what is actually known: "Eleven agents cost roughly eleven times one agent's output. What one agent walking the same eleven checklists would cost has not been measured here; do not assume it is an eleventh, because a single long conversation carries all eleven checklists in its context at once."

findings.title: The five-run table cannot be checked by anyone, and its own rows contradict each other
findings.where: Lines 375-379 (the five data rows) and the caption at lines 361-370
findings.problem: The table gives one token column and two money columns, and no reader can get from the first to the second: the input/output split is absent, and the cache-read count — which the arithmetic above shows is over half the bill — has no column. Worse, the rows are mutually inconsistent on their face. 24 Aug (1,700,364 tokens → $30) has 4.8% FEWER billable tokens than 17 Aug (1,786,769 → $16) and costs 87.5% more: $17.64 per million billable against $8.95. Across the five rows the implied rate swings from $8.95/M to $17.64/M with no explanation offered. A skeptical reader concludes either that the token column is decorative or that the money column is wrong, and the footer confirms they cannot settle it — "That log is not yet published... the table is checkable only by someone with the file." Meanwhile line 351 promises in bold "You can go and look at the task before you judge the price" and line 354 says "It matters that this is checkable." The retraction is in 12.5px grey type 190 lines below the promise.
findings.fix: Add two columns — output tokens and cache reads — so each row's arithmetic closes, or drop the token column entirely and present the dollar range alone. And move the footer's "the log is not yet published" admission into the caption, where the checkability claim is made.

findings.title: "Measured, not estimated" — the vendor's own doc calls this exact method an estimate
findings.where: Lines 347-348: "one real, repeated task, measured rather than estimated"; line 412: "The receipt is on the usage screen."
findings.problem: The figures are harness-reported token counts multiplied by list rates. The page's own linked source (code.claude.com/docs/en/costs, line 477) says of precisely this: "Claude Code computes the dollar figure locally from token counts at list price... The figure is an estimate, so for authoritative billing see the Usage page in the Claude Console." The page then closes the same section by telling the reader the receipt is on the usage screen — while its own centrepiece has never been put next to one. The caption half-concedes this ("Computed, not read off an invoice") and the footer fully concedes it ("are not invoices"), which makes "measured rather than estimated" at line 347 the one place the page overclaims, and it is the sentence introducing the whole example. A vendor's pricing lead reading this would note that the page is teaching a discipline it exempts itself from.
findings.fix: Change line 347-348 to "one real, repeated task, counted from the tool's own token log rather than guessed — and computed at list rates, not read off an invoice." Then reconcile one run against the Console usage page and say what the gap was; that single number would make this section unanswerable.

findings.title: A "ceiling" of four rounds, disproved in the next sentence and left unpriced
findings.where: Lines 399-403: "the ceiling for one document is four rounds — call it $64–160... One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it."
findings.problem: $64–160 is arithmetically right (4 × the $16–40 per-round Opus range). But a ceiling that a recorded run passed by 3.5× is not a ceiling, and the page declines to do the one multiplication that matters: 14 rounds × $16–40 = $224–560. The reader is handed the reassuring number in bold and the alarming one as a bare round-count with no dollars attached, in a section whose stated purpose is that "it can also run away." That is convenient in exactly the direction that sells the page. It also sits badly against line 342's "$150–250 per developer per month" — one unattended document can outspend a heavy engineer's entire month.
findings.fix: Price the real event: "the process caps at four rounds — $64–160 at the larger model's rates. One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it, which is $224–560 for a single document. Nothing was broken. Nobody was watching." And say whether the four-round cap existed when that run happened.

findings.title: The cost-driver section omits caching and so contradicts the page's own table by 5.6×
findings.where: Line 461: "Your entire conversation is re-sent on every single request. A one-line question in a session you have had open all day carries the whole day with it."
findings.problem: Re-sent, yes; re-billed at full price, no. The linked Anthropic doc states it explicitly: "With prompt caching, Claude Code re-reads that history at the cached token rate." The page knows this — its own caption charges cache reads at a tenth. Price the 28 Aug run under the mental model line 461 gives a reader: (1,359,900 + 26,384,348) × $5/M + 236,512 × $25/M = $144.63, against the $25.90 the table actually charges. The page's explanation of the cost model overstates its own worked example by 5.6×. A researcher who believes line 461 will also draw the wrong operational conclusion, since a fresh session discards a warm cache and can cost more on related work, not less — while line 461 calls starting fresh "the largest lever you have" with no evidence for the ranking.
findings.fix: Add to the sub-line: "Most of that re-sent history is billed at a tenth of the normal input rate, because it is cached — on the measured run above, 95% of input tokens were cache reads, and they were still half the bill. Long sessions cost less than they look, and more than a short one." And either source the "largest lever" ranking or soften it to "one of the largest."

findings.title: A per-seat monthly stipend prorated down to ninety minutes is not a budget
findings.where: Lines 421-423: "sizes its classroom allocation per user per month, for a term... an order of $5–15 a student — $30–90 for the room"; line 434: "A plan is a ceiling you have bought whether or not you reach it"
findings.problem: The page states the commitment unit — per user, per month, for a term — and then prices below it. You cannot buy a twentieth of a seat-month. At the $50/user/month figure the page cites, the minimum real commitment for six students is $300 for one month, or $1,200 across a four-month term, to run one ninety-minute session. The reader is told on line 433-434 to "Budget with the first number" and the first number is $30–90 — off by 3–13× from anything a finance office can actually provision. The flag at lines 441-451 covers the $50 being unconfirmed but never touches this, which is the structural error and does not depend on the $50 at all. Separately, points.md §F calls this a "stipend" — something received, possibly as a grant — while line 434 calls it a plan "you have bought." If it is a grant the marginal cost is $0 and the whole plan-versus-meter contrast this section is built on does not apply to this case.
findings.fix: Replace the derivation with the provisionable unit: "You cannot buy part of a seat-month. Six students at the reported $50/user/month is $300 for one month and $1,200 across a term — that is what has to be committed to hold one ninety-minute session, even though the session itself will consume a few dollars." And say plainly whether the classroom allocation is bought or granted.

findings.title: "Often it is not cheaper" is unsourced and contradicted by the page's own numbers
findings.where: Line 284: "Not because it is cheaper — often it is not"
findings.problem: On a page that dates every figure and flags every estimate, the one comparative claim that decides where a reader's money goes carries no support at all. And the page's own data points the other way: it establishes that a serious task runs $6–40 on a meter (line 384) and that Claude Pro is $20/month (line 308-310). One review on a meter costs more than a month of the subscription. The page never puts those two of its own numbers side by side — which is the single most decision-relevant comparison a cost-anxious reader could be handed, and its absence makes "a meter is the correct choice for some people" (line 285) look like even-handedness with nothing behind it. A skeptical department head asks the obvious question and the page has no answer.
findings.fix: Either support the claim (name the usage pattern where the meter wins, e.g. very light or very bursty use where a $20/month floor goes unused) or drop "often it is not" and say what the numbers say: "often it is also cheaper — one meter-priced review of the kind below costs more than a month of the $20 tier. The reason to buy a ceiling is the failure mode; the price usually agrees."

findings.title: The staleness banner is the one check on the page that cannot fail
findings.where: Line 226: "Treat the numbers as orders of magnitude and the links as the authority."
findings.problem: An order of magnitude is 10×. Read literally, the banner licenses $26 to mean anything from $2.60 to $260, and $30–90 for the room to mean $3 to $900 — which pre-forgives every error on the page, including the ones above, and makes the whole document unfalsifiable. No reader can ever come back and say a figure was wrong. It also sits oddly against the precision on display: seven-significant-figure token counts (3,141,042) under an instruction to treat everything as a power of ten. The banner is doing real work about link rot and plan renaming, but as written it is a blanket indemnity, and a hostile reader will spend it on whichever number they dislike.
findings.fix: Scope it to what actually decays: "Plan names and prices move; treat those as approximate and check the vendor's page. The measured token counts and the arithmetic below do not decay — if they are wrong, they were wrong on the day."

findings.title: The stated four-round ceiling is disproved two sentences later
findings.where: Lines 399–403: "the ceiling for one document is four rounds — call it $64–160 at the larger model's rates. One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it."
findings.problem: The page hands a cost-anxious reader a hard number to budget against — a ceiling of four rounds, $64–160 — and then, in the next sentence, narrates a run at fourteen rounds. Both cannot be true. The arithmetic makes the size of the miss plain: the five measured runs cost $16–40 each at Opus rates, so four rounds is $64–160 as stated, but fourteen rounds is $224–560, which is 3.5x the ceiling the reader was just told to expect. A reader budgeting from the bolded figure would be short by up to $400 on a single document. The rhetorical build ("Nothing was broken. Nobody was watching.") is excellent and should stay; it is the unexplained contradiction in front of it that is the defect.
findings.fix: Say which claim is true and why the other happened. Either the cap is configured and was off in the recorded run — "the process can be capped at four rounds, call it $64–160; the run that went fourteen had no cap set, and cost roughly $224–560" — or there is no cap and the "ceiling" language must go entirely. Do not leave both numbers standing unreconciled.

findings.title: The footer provenance paragraph is the one paragraph that could be cut
findings.where: Line 541, the paragraph beginning "The five-run worked example is derived from a token log in"
findings.problem: Almost every clause in this 190-word paragraph has already been said on the page, usually verbatim. "Prices and plan shapes read from the vendors' own pages on 29 August 2026" repeats the caption at line 292 and the banner at line 225. "The teaching-session figures are estimates and are labeled as such" repeats line 441. "$50 from secondary coverage, and the university's own page states no amount" repeats lines 443–445 almost word for word. "The two money columns ... are the same tokens priced at two different models ... and not two subscription plans" repeats lines 366–370 for the third time on one page. "nothing re-checks them" repeats line 226's "Nothing on this page re-checks itself." The effect is that the page's carefulness, which is its best quality, starts to read as anxiety — and the two facts here that are genuinely new (the log is unpublished; the university facts are generalised from one institution) are buried in the middle of the restatements.
findings.fix: Cut to the two sentences that appear nowhere else: that the token log behind the five-run table is not yet published, so the table is checkable only by someone with the file; and that the institutional and student-credit facts were checked at one university on 27 August 2026 and generalised. Delete the rest — the captions and the banner already carry it.

findings.title: The five-run caption states the same cache-rate caveat twice in one caption
findings.where: Lines 361–370: "with cache reads charged at a tenth of the input rate" ... and, 40 words later, "with cached reading charged at a tenth of the input rate"
findings.problem: One caption, 130 words, longer than the five-row table it explains, and it repeats its own central caveat inside itself in slightly different words — which reads less like emphasis than like two drafts that were merged and never reconciled. It also dates itself twice ("on 29 August 2026" at the start, "on 29 August 2026" again in the model-rates clause). A reader trying to understand a table has to get through a paragraph first, and a reader who notices the doubling starts to wonder what else was pasted rather than written.
findings.fix: One pass, one statement of each fact: five complete runs across three projects, summed per run from the tool's own token log on 29 August 2026; dollars computed from those counts at list rates, cache reads at a tenth of input; the runs used different models, so the columns are a band, not a price. Roughly half the current length.

findings.title: The caption defends a column header the table does not have
findings.where: Line 369: "**"Tier" here means the model, not the plan** — the plans in the table above are a different thing that unfortunately shares the word."
findings.problem: The table's headers are "Run | Billable tokens | At Opus-5 rates | At Sonnet-5 rates" (line 372). The word "Tier" appears nowhere in it. The disclaimer is an orphan from an earlier version of the table, and it now creates the confusion it was written to prevent: a reader hunts for a "Tier" column, fails to find one, and is left unsure whether they are looking at the right table. The immediately preceding sentence — "The two money columns are the same tokens priced at two different models, not two subscription plans" — already does the whole job, and does it against the headers that actually exist.
findings.fix: Delete the "Tier" sentence outright. The column names Opus-5 and Sonnet-5 plus the preceding sentence already make the point.

findings.title: The maintainer's voice keeps surfacing in a student handout
findings.where: Line 417 "The one case anybody here has costed"; line 439 "which is the opposite of the conclusion this material reached before anyone actually looked"; line 450 "**One measured session is still owed**"; line 541 "a handoff asking for it has gone to that project"
findings.problem: These are project-ledger sentences that have been lifted from author-facing notes (they read almost verbatim from points.md §F) into a page addressed to a nervous faculty member. That reader has no idea what conclusion "this material" previously reached, who "anybody here" is, who is owed a measured session, or what a handoff to another project is. Each one asks them to hold a piece of the project's internal history in order to parse a sentence about money. It is a register break in a page that is otherwise disciplined about speaking to the reader, and it is worst at line 439, which ends a strong section on an inside joke.
findings.fix: Rewrite each in the reader's frame. Line 439: end at "the decision becomes a pedagogical one" and stop. Line 450: "Nobody has yet measured a real session" — the obligation is a fact, not a debt. Line 417: "The one case that has been costed at all". Line 541: "the token log behind this table is not yet published", without the handoff.

findings.title: "Every one of these" opens a section with no antecedent
findings.where: Line 260: "Every one of these is sold in one of three shapes, and the shape matters more than the number."
findings.problem: The nearest plural before "these" is the list of permanently free things — git, GitHub, an editor, hosting — which are precisely the things that are not sold at all. The heading above ("The one thing that costs: the agent") is singular, so "these" has nothing to attach to and the reader has to reverse into it. It is the first sentence of the section the whole page is built around, and it makes the reader work before it has earned the right to.
findings.fix: Name the referent: "Agents are sold in one of three shapes, and the shape matters more than the number." The rest of the paragraph — "nobody will tell you unprompted" — is good and needs nothing.

findings.title: The page narrates its own structure five times
findings.where: Line 206 "This is the whole of the rest of this page"; line 341 "the mistake this section exists to prevent"; line 411 "If you take one thing from this page"; line 419 "the disagreement is the whole argument of this page in miniature"; line 437 "Either way the conclusion is the same and it is the point of this section"
findings.problem: Individually each is a defensible signpost. Five of them in one handout becomes a tic, and it flattens emphasis: when the page declares four different things to be its point, its argument, and its one takeaway, none of them lands as the point. Line 419's "the whole argument of this page in miniature" is the most inflated — it promises the reader a synthesis and then delivers two estimates that disagree, which is interesting but is not the whole argument of anything.
findings.fix: Keep one. Line 411 ("a number an agent gives you about its own consumption is a claim, not a receipt") earns its billing and should be the only sentence that claims takeaway status. Cut the framing clause from 419 and 437 and let the content assert itself; both paragraphs are strong enough without being introduced.

findings.title: A flourish clause that reverses the sentence it ends
findings.where: Line 210: "which is the same reason 2.3 tells you to keep the data root out of the sync client — a rule that is about reliability and happens to also be the thing keeping this line cheap."
findings.problem: This is the sound-good-say-little sentence of the page. It is inside a sub-line of a bullet that has already covered the free tier, the review folder, the exception, and the paid price; by the time the reader reaches "happens to also be the thing keeping this line cheap" they are four clauses deep in a footnote. The word order ("happens to also be") is awkward, and the clause actually undercuts the sentence before it: the cross-reference to 2.3 was made to explain a cost consequence, and the coda then says the rule is not really about cost.
findings.fix: End the sentence at "keep the data root out of the sync client." The cross-reference does the work; the reflection on why the rule exists belongs in Cold Start 2.3, not here.

findings.title: "Some organizations" is the only unsourced claim on a page that dates everything
findings.where: Line 511: "Some organizations have gone as far as ranking people by token consumption"
findings.problem: Every other assertion on this page carries a date, a link, or an explicit admission that it is an estimate — that discipline is the page's main claim on the reader's trust. This sentence, in the section explicitly labelled "the uncomfortable one", rests on an anonymous "some organizations" with no source at all. A sceptical reader who has been trained by the previous 400 lines to look for the citation will notice its absence exactly where the page is at its most rhetorical, which is the worst possible place to spend credibility.
findings.fix: Either attribute it ("reported at least once in …") or convert it to the conditional the argument actually needs: "Where token consumption is ranked or made visible, the ranking measures budget and confidence, not work." The closing line — "If a number is going to be visible, make it the work" — survives either way and should.

findings.title: "Billable tokens" column omits the tokens that are half the bill
findings.where: Line 372 header "Billable tokens"; lines 384–386 "Between 10.8 and 36.9 million further tokens were read back out of cache on top of those figures"
findings.problem: Cache reads are billable — at a tenth of input, but billed. For the 28 Aug run the source log (OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1) gives output 236,512 + new input 1,359,900 + cache creation 1,014 = the 1,597,426 in the table, and 26,384,348 cache-read tokens excluded from it. Priced at Opus rates: $5.91 output + $6.80 input + $13.19 cache reads = $25.90, which is the $26 in the table. So 50.9% of the money sits outside the column headed "Billable tokens", and the dollar figures already include it. The sentence "on top of those figures" sits immediately after "costs somewhere between $6 and $40", so the nearest antecedent is the dollars — telling the reader the price is an undercount when it is not. A researcher who reads this and then estimates their own cost from a token counter that reports the same column will be low by roughly 10–17×.
findings.fix: Rename the column "Tokens excl. cache reads" (or show cache reads as a fourth column), and rewrite the sentence to say the opposite of what it currently implies: "The dollar figures already include a further 10.8–36.9 million tokens read back out of cache at a tenth of the input rate — on the 28 Aug run that cache reading was $13 of the $26."

findings.title: A "ceiling" of four rounds, disproved in the next sentence, with no replacement number
findings.where: Lines 399–403: "the ceiling for one document is four rounds — call it $64–160 … One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it."
findings.problem: Four rounds is not a ceiling if a run went fourteen; the page states as a bound something it then reports being exceeded by 3.5×, and gives no revised figure. This is the runaway-cost paragraph on a page written for readers who are anxious about runaway cost, and it is the one place where the actual worst observed number belongs. At the page's own $16–40 per round, fourteen rounds is $224–560 — a number that changes whether someone points a departmental billing code at this, and it is the only number on the page that is withheld.
findings.fix: State it: "The process is supposed to stop at four rounds — call it $64–160. One recorded run went fourteen before a person stopped it, which at the same rates is $224–560. The cap is a setting, not a wall." Then say what actually stopped it (a person, not the software), because that is the operative fact.

findings.title: "An eleventh as much" is arithmetically impossible on the page's own data
findings.where: Lines 394–398: "Eleven agents cost roughly eleven times one agent … One agent walking the same eleven checklists costs an eleventh as much"
findings.problem: Eleven checklists produce eleven sets of findings whether one agent or eleven writes them, and output tokens do not shrink when you consolidate. In the measured run output was 236,512 tokens = $5.91 of the $25.90 total, or 22.8%. So even if the consolidated version's input were free, its floor is about one quarter of the parallel cost, not one eleventh. "Eleven times one agent" is also not a thing the data supports: per-role billable ranges 100,369–186,886 (1.9×) and per-role cache reads 965,722–5,398,562 (5.6×), so there is no single "one agent" to multiply. The argument for independence does not need this claim and is weakened by resting on a number that does not survive division.
findings.fix: Replace the multiplier with the measured shape: "Eleven independent readers cost several times one reader — not eleven times, because the eleven reports get written either way and writing is the expensive half. On the run above, output alone was $6 of the $26." The independence argument stands on its own without a fabricated ratio.

findings.title: Output tokens — 5× the price of input — are missing from the list of what drives the bill
findings.where: Lines 458–475, the four-item list under "What actually drives the number"
findings.problem: On every rate the page cites, output costs five times input ($25 vs $5; $10 vs $2), and reasoning/thinking tokens are billed as output. In the page's own measured run, output was 14.8% of the tokens in that column but 46.5% of the non-cache money. None of the four levers mentions this. A researcher following this list concludes that conversation length and model choice are the whole story, and will not connect "asked it to rewrite the whole file rather than tell me what to change" or "asked for maximum reasoning effort on an easy question" to their bill — both of which are direct, free, quality-neutral savings.
findings.fix: Add a fifth item, ranked second or third: "How much you ask it to write. Answers cost five times what questions cost, and the model's own reasoning is billed as writing. 'Tell me which three lines to change' is cheaper than 'give me the corrected file' — and easier to check."

findings.title: Caching is presented as a permanent discount; it is perishable, and that is the real mechanism behind lever 1
findings.where: Line 461 "Your entire conversation is re-sent on every single request … Starting a fresh session between unrelated tasks costs nothing"; the caption's "cache reads charged at a tenth of the input rate" (lines 363–369)
findings.problem: The re-send is real, but the page never says the re-sent part is normally served from cache at a tenth — which is why its own run cost $26 rather than $145 (26,384,348 cache-read tokens at full input rate would be $131.92 instead of $13.19, a 5.6× difference). More consequentially, the page presents the tenth as a static fact when it is a perishable one: the cache has a short time-to-live (five minutes by default on Anthropic, refreshed while you work), so the same long session is cheap while you are typing and re-pays full input price for the entire history on the first message after a coffee break or a meeting. That is the actionable, non-obvious fact, and its absence means readers will fear the wrong thing (long sessions) and not recognise the real one (interrupted long sessions). "Starting a fresh session costs nothing" is also not quite true — a fresh session re-reads the project context at full price, or at the 1.25× cache-write rate.
findings.fix: Rewrite lever 1: "Your whole conversation is re-sent every request, but a warm cache charges a tenth for the repeat — on the run above that was $13 instead of $131. The cache goes cold in minutes. Come back after lunch and the next message re-pays full price for the whole day. So the rule is not 'short sessions', it is 'finish a task, then start a new session' — which costs a little, not nothing."

findings.title: Lever ordering ranks a 2.5× quality-costing lever above an 11× free one
findings.where: Line 456 "Four things move it, in roughly this order"; lines 464–466 (model, ranked 2) and 468–469 (agents, ranked 3)
findings.problem: By the page's own table, model choice is exactly 2.5× ($40 vs $16, $26 vs $10 — Opus 5 $5/$25 against Sonnet 5 $2/$10). Agent count in the same worked example is 11×, and rounds reached 14×. So the page ranks the smallest multiplier — and the only one of the four that is paid for in answer quality — above the two largest, both of which are free. "The largest models cost several times the smaller ones" also overstates 2.5× as "several".
