A cost-anxious researcher following this order downgrades their model first, gets worse answers, and leaves the 11× and 14× levers untouched.
findings.fix: Reorder to context, fan-out, output, then model, and say why model is last: "Which model. The gap is about 2.5×, not the order of magnitude people expect, and it is the only lever on this list you pay for in quality. Pull the other three first."

findings.title: Every dollar in the worked example is a meter dollar, on a page that tells most readers to buy a ceiling
findings.where: Lines 384–390 ("$6 and $40", "a few dollars for a serious piece of work"); line 412 "The receipt is on the usage screen"; line 521 "If it is your own money, buy a ceiling."
findings.problem: The five-run table prices tokens at API list rates — that is shape 2. The page's own advice sends most readers to shape 1, and on a subscription that eleven-agent review costs zero additional dollars and instead consumes allowance until it stops. The page never makes the translation, so the reader it is addressing cannot use its central number: they do not know whether "$26" means twenty-six dollars or roughly a third of today's allowance. The same gap breaks the page's best line — for a subscription user the agent's own usage screen reports API-equivalent dollars that appear on no statement, so "the receipt is on the usage screen" is true for shape 2 and 3 and misleading for shape 1, where the meaningful reading is the limit indicator, not the dollar figure.
findings.fix: Add one sentence after the $6–$40 conclusion: "That is the meter price. On a subscription the same review costs no extra money — it spends allowance, and $26 of tokens is roughly how much of a month you just used. Which sentence applies to you is the whole of the plan-versus-meter distinction." And branch line 412: on a ceiling, the receipt is the limit screen; the dollar figure the tool shows you is a list-price equivalent nobody bills.

findings.title: The spend-limit advice never says what hitting a spend limit looks like
findings.where: Lines 525–526: "set the spend limit the same day … stops the only genuinely bad outcome on this page"
findings.problem: Setting a spend limit is right, but it converts a meter into a ceiling with a materially worse failure mode than a subscription's, and the page describes none of it. A limit hit mid-run does not pause politely: work stops part-way through a task, and in a fan-out of the kind this page just spent a page describing, some agents finish and others die, leaving a result that looks complete and is not. This project's own records carry a candidate instance — OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1's scope note reports seven of eleven reviewers dying mid-run on a monthly spending limit (flagged there as uncorroborated). Advising the control without describing its failure mode leaves a reader unable to recognise it when it happens.
findings.fix: Add to the sub-line: "Know what hitting it looks like: work stops where it is, not at a tidy boundary. If several agents were running, some finish and some do not, and the result can look finished. Treat an unexpectedly short answer near month end as a billing symptom, not a quality one."

findings.title: Subscription worst case stated as hours; these plans meter on more than one clock
findings.where: Line 267 "Worst case: you cannot work for a few hours." and line 284 "you stop for four hours"
findings.problem: The page tells readers to go and check the vendor's page for every price, then asserts a reset period without doing so. Current consumer plans on both vendors named meter against a short rolling window and a longer weekly one, so the worst case is not bounded by a few hours — a weekly cap means days, and it lands during exactly the sustained push that triggers it. This matters most for the reader the page is trying to reassure: someone deciding whether to run a class or hit a deadline on a $20 ceiling.
findings.fix: Soften to what is checkable and add the second clock: "Worst case: you stop until it resets — usually hours, but these plans also carry a longer limit, so check what the reset actually says before you plan a deadline around it." Apply the same edit at line 284 rather than repeating "four hours" as a fact.

findings.title: The five-run table drops the "this is a floor" caveat its source prescribes
findings.where: Line 384: "So: reviewing one document properly costs somewhere between $6 and $40."
findings.problem: `docs/cases/OPEN-CORRECTIONS.md` C1 is the owner of these token figures, and its correction table (line 25) prescribes a third edit that this page has not carried: "that the figure counts **the eleven reviewers only** — the session that spawns them, reads eleven reports and writes the record is not in it, so the number is a floor". The handout takes C1's numbers verbatim (1,597,426 matches C1 line 58 exactly; the five-run range 1.6–3.1M and median ~1.8M match C1 line 61) but presents the derived dollars as the cost of the review rather than a floor. Every downstream figure inherits it — "$64–160" for four rounds, "a few dollars for a serious piece of work", and the teaching-session meter estimate that is explicitly extrapolated "at the per-task rates established above". A reader budgeting from this page is budgeting from a number its own source says is incomplete.
findings.fix: Add the caveat to the caption or the sentence at line 384, in C1's own terms: the counts are the eleven reviewers only — the session that spawns them, reads eleven reports and writes the record is not included, so $6–40 is a floor.

findings.title: Sponsored keys stated as fact; source flags it as the least verified line it has
findings.where: Line 487: "A graduate student employed as a research or teaching assistant can often be sponsored; a student on a taught course generally cannot."
findings.problem: `points.md` §F (lines 839–842) is the source, and it ends that bullet with "⚠ *Single source, read once, not confirmed on a second page. It is the most decision-relevant line found and the least verified.*" The handout carries the claim, hardens "the FAQ indicates" into "can often be sponsored", and drops the ⚠ entirely. This is the one line on the page a faculty reader will act on when deciding whether a cohort can be covered — the source says so in as many words — and it is the one line whose provenance the page hides. The footer flags the teaching-session estimate and the unpublished token log but says nothing about this.
findings.fix: Restore the hedge inline: say it comes from a single FAQ line, read once, not confirmed on a second page — and that it is the most decision-relevant and least verified fact in the section. Or drop the claim until it is confirmed.

findings.title: "Nothing was broken" contradicts the source's account of the same fourteen-round run
findings.where: Lines 402–403: "One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it. Nothing was broken. Nobody was watching."
findings.problem: The source for this run is `docs/cases/2026-08-28-the-tests-were-defending-the-bug.md` Point 5, which says of that same run: "a review that ran **fourteen** rounds before a human stopped it — and, in the same run, seven of the eleven reviewers **died mid-run on a monthly spending limit** and had to be re-run a cheaper way." So something did break, and what broke was a ceiling doing exactly what Shape 1 (line 266, "When you have used your allowance, it stops") promises. The page drops the single best real-world illustration of its own central framing and replaces it with an assertion the source contradicts. `OPEN-CORRECTIONS.md` C1 (line 77) adds the honest qualifier the page could reuse: the fourteen-round count is corroborated by a `rounds: 14` record, but "the spending-limit detail rests on the retelling."
findings.fix: Either restore the spending-limit half with C1's qualifier — a ceiling stopped seven of eleven reviewers mid-run, on a retold account — or delete "Nothing was broken", which is not supported by any source in the repo.

findings.title: The cost-driver list re-derives §10's and drops its headline rule
findings.where: Lines 458–475, the four items under "What actually drives the number"
findings.problem: `course-outline.md` §10 line 419 already owns this list, ordered, under "Where it actually goes, in rough order": long sessions, **re-reading** ("A file pasted or read into the room is paid for again on every subsequent turn, not once. Ask for the part you need rather than the file you have"), fan-out, and **work a command does exactly** — which §10 marks as "the one that deserves a rule" and then states: "**The rule: if the answer is exactly computable, compute it.**" The handout keeps items 1 and 3, substitutes "which model" and "vagueness", and loses both re-reading and the compute-it rule. That rule is the cheapest lever on the list for a non-programmer, it is free rather than a trade-off, and §10 uses it to tie the cost material back to the course's own thesis about mechanisms. A student-facing cost sheet is the natural place for it and it is the one thing the sheet does not say.
findings.fix: Reuse §10's list rather than inventing a parallel one: add "work a command does exactly — if the answer is exactly computable, compute it" as a fifth item, and fold §10's re-reading point ("ask for the part you need rather than the file you have") into the vagueness item.

findings.title: Driver 1 is near-verbatim from cold-start 4.6, minus the clause that matters
findings.where: Line 461: "Your entire conversation is re-sent on every single request. A one-line question in a session you have had open all day carries the whole day with it."
findings.problem: `docs/handouts/cold-start.html` line 777 — the step this page sends the reader to at line 477 — says: "Your whole conversation is re-sent on every single request. A one-line question in a session you have had open all day still carries the whole day with it, **and coming back after a long break re-processes the lot.** Which makes `/clear` between unrelated tasks the largest single lever you have, and it costs nothing." The handout reproduces the sentence with "whole"→"entire", drops the long-break clause, and replaces the actual command `/clear` with the vaguer "starting a fresh session". The dropped clause is the caching mechanism, which `course-outline.md` line 417 insists on carrying ("Caching cuts part of this when turns come quickly, and how much depends on the plan and on the gap between turns") — and which this page's own table depends on, since "10.8 and 36.9 million further tokens" of cache reads at a tenth rate are most of what the runs cost. Two sheets in the same system now state the same fact differently, neither points at the other, and the shorter one lost the half a reader acts on.
findings.fix: Either cross-reference cold-start 4.6 instead of restating it, or restore both dropped pieces: the long-break re-processing clause and the literal `/clear`.

findings.title: Ownership of the access material is now split between §F and this page, with no pointer either way
findings.where: Line 491 ("Student credit programs have borders") and line 487; footer line 541
findings.problem: `HANDOFF.md` line 22 still names `points.md` **§F** as the owner: "Access, cost, routes, rates | `points.md` §F — sourced and dated 2026-08-27", and §F itself (line 796) says "Extract it the moment there is a better home." This page is that better home, but it extracted only part: it takes the $100 Codex credits and the Claude Code employment check, and leaves behind three routes §F records with dates and quotes — the Shortcode blocker (§F line 833, which blocks the Toolkit, Claude Code and classroom provisioning in one stroke, and which the author does not have), Claude Campus (§F line 845, "applications closed" as of 2026-08-26), and Anthropic AI for Science (§F line 846: up to **$20,000** in API credits over six months, reviewed the first Monday of each month, prioritising biology and life sciences). For an audience of academic researchers, that last one is arguably the most valuable line in §F, and a section headed "Student credit programs have borders" that names one programme reads as a survey when it is a sample of one.
findings.fix: Either name §F as the source and say this page is a summary of it, or complete the extraction: add the Shortcode blocker, the closed Campus programme, and AI for Science with their dates. Then update `HANDOFF.md` line 22 to say which document is now the owner.

findings.title: Shape 3 drops the sentence that ties cost to the course's own thesis
findings.where: Lines 276–280, "Shape 3 — somebody else's meter"
findings.problem: `points.md` D2 (lines 540–547) is the source of this fork and states the conclusion the page never reaches: "a ceiling is a crude mechanism but it is a mechanism; a Shortcode is a request that the spender be sensible, and B4 is about what happens to requests." That is the whole cost sheet reduced to one line, in the course's own established vocabulary, and it is the reason the ceiling/meter choice is a teaching point rather than a budgeting tip. The handout instead argues it from feedback latency ("the feedback arrives weeks later"). Note the sibling sheet has the same gap: `cold-start.html` line 429 also restates D2's fork ("A personal plan is an allowance… An institutional billing code is usually uncapped: nothing stops, nothing warns") without it.
findings.fix: Add D2's line to the note at 284–286: a ceiling is a crude mechanism but it is a mechanism; a billing code is a request that the spender be sensible, and the rest of the course is about what happens to requests.

findings.title: The $50 figure is attributed to the wrong page, and "stipend" has become "allocation"
findings.where: Line 444: "The per-user monthly allocation is reported as $50 in secondary coverage; the university’s own pricing page states no amount."
findings.problem: `points.md` §F line 831 says: "⚠ *A stipend of $50/user/month appears in secondary coverage; the ITS page itself states no amount.*" — and "the ITS page" there is the Codex for the Classroom page, the subject of that bullet. The university's **pricing** page is a different page in §F (line 816) and it does state amounts: "`claude-opus-5` **$5.00 / $25.00** per 1M tokens… `claude-sonnet-5` $2.00 / $10.00." A reader who follows the page's own advice and goes to look will find the pricing page full of numbers. Separately, §F and `OPEN-FINDINGS.md` N1 are careful that "allotment/allocation" is a loaded word here — N1 line 155 records that "'What is the allotment' presumed a ceiling that is not there" on the faculty path — so recasting a classroom *stipend* as an *allocation* on lines 422 and 444 blurs a distinction the sources were corrected into making.
findings.fix: Say which page was checked — the classroom-programme page, not the pricing page — and restore §F's word, "stipend".

findings.title: The footer overstates how long the five-run table stays checkable
findings.where: Line 541: "That log is not yet published — a handoff asking for it has gone to that project, and until it lands the table is checkable only by someone with the file."
findings.problem: `OPEN-CORRECTIONS.md` C1's provenance block (lines 82–89) carries two things this sentence drops. First, the check does not need the file: "the numbers are still checkable the way they were derived: run the tool against the transcripts" — and it names the tool, `metrics/measure_review_cost.py` in `syncytium2/murderboard`, which the page already links. Second, and more important, the window closes: "while the transcripts exist. **The harness prunes them.**" The handout implies a check that is merely inconvenient today; the source says it is a check with an expiry date. That is the page's own thesis about staleness, and it is the one claim on the page where the source is more alarming than the copy.
findings.fix: Replace with C1's version: the table is reproducible by running `metrics/measure_review_cost.py` against the subagent transcripts, for as long as the harness has not pruned them — and the branches carrying the CSV are still local-only.

findings.title: The course's own loop is renamed in a phrase set as a quotation
findings.where: Line 484: "Since the entire method is spec, check, re-spec"
findings.problem: The canonical form throughout the repo is "spec, validate, re-spec" — `points.md` B6 line 253, `course-outline.md` §3 line 226, `course-outline-external.md` line 63, and both sibling handouts: `search-to-shipped.html` line 642 ("Spec, validate, re-spec.") and `four-barriers.html` line 730 ("Spec, validate, re-spec. Re-spec is the normal case, not the failure case."). This page italicises a third variant, which reads as a quotation of a named thing that is named differently everywhere else a student will encounter it — including on the two sheets handed out beside this one.
findings.fix: Change to "spec, validate, re-spec".

findings.title: Two repo documents still carry the price estimate this page supersedes
findings.where: Lines 375–379, the five-run table
findings.problem: `OPEN-FINDINGS.md` N1 (line 161) records "What one full run consumes… **Still open.** One run, then read the usage back", and reasons from an estimate at line 163: "eleven roles at roughly 12k in / 2k out each is about **$1.20 a round**, so a three-round run lands in single digits of dollars." `HANDOFF.md` §5 (line 93) repeats it: "**Still outstanding: one measured run.** The arithmetic says single-digit dollars." This page's measured figure for an eleven-role round is $16–40 at Opus rates — roughly 20× that estimate — and it does not say it is answering N1, while N1 and HANDOFF do not say they have been answered. A maintainer reading the repo cannot tell which of the two is current, which is the exact failure mode the page itself warns about at lines 224–227.
findings.fix: Add one line to the caption or footer noting that these runs are the measurement `OPEN-FINDINGS.md` N1 asks for, and close or annotate N1 and `HANDOFF.md` §5 in the same commit so the superseded $1.20/round arithmetic is not left standing.

findings.title: "Agent" is the subject of the page and is never defined
findings.where: Line 205, "The agent — free tiers exist and are real"; relied on again at line 488, "the institution itself draws a line between chat and agent"
findings.problem: The word arrives in the first list item as a thing that costs money, and by line 260 it is "every one of these" — plural, unenumerated. I never learn what an agent is, what it does, or how it differs from the chat box I have used. Line 488 then makes the chat/agent distinction load-bearing for the equity argument ("a better demonstration of the difference between the two than any classroom demo") while assuming I already hold that difference. Someone deciding whether to assign this to students is being asked to price a thing the page never names.
findings.fix: One clause at first use, line 205: "The agent — the program that reads and writes files on your machine, as opposed to a chat box you paste into." That single contrast also does the work line 488 currently assumes.

findings.title: Jargon inherited from Cold Start that this sheet never unpacks
findings.where: Line 210, "keep the data root out of the sync client"; line 484, "the entire method is spec, check, re-spec"
findings.problem: Both sentences carry real weight and both stop a cold reader. "Data root" and "sync client" are Cold Start vocabulary; here they sit inside a parenthetical justifying why storage stays cheap, so I cannot skip them and still follow the money. "Spec, check, re-spec" does more damage: it is the premise of the whole free-tier equity argument ("a person with fewer attempts is not doing a slightly worse version of the work"), so if I do not know what a spec is, the most important paragraph on the page is an assertion I have to take on faith.
findings.fix: Line 210: "keep your data folder outside the folder Dropbox watches". Line 484: gloss it once — "the entire method is write down what you want, check what came back, write it down again better".

findings.title: "The record" is promised in the free list and never appears in it
findings.where: Line 222, "the record, the history, the editor, and somewhere to put a web page"
findings.problem: That sentence sets up four free things and reads as a table of contents for the section immediately below. The section then lists git ("the thing that keeps the history"), a GitHub account, an editor, and hosting. Three of the four map cleanly; "the record" has no entry. I spent a paragraph working out whether the record is GitHub, a fifth thing I had missed, or the history under a second name. On a page whose promise is "here is everything you will be charged for", an item that appears in the summary and vanishes from the list reads like an omission, not a synonym.
findings.fix: Either name it in the list — make the GitHub bullet "A GitHub account, the shared copy of the record" — or drop "the record" from line 222 so the summary and the list have the same four members.

findings.title: "Ceiling" carries four different meanings, two of them contradictory
findings.where: Line 264 "Shape 1 — a ceiling"; lines 320 and 330 (Shape column: storage and a domain both marked "Ceiling"); line 342 "roughly the ceiling of what a single very heavy human being can spend"; line 400 "the ceiling for one document is four rounds"
findings.problem: This is the collision that cost me the most. Shape 1 defines a ceiling precisely and memorably: "When you have used your allowance, it stops and tells you when it resets." Stopping is the whole definition — it is why line 284 tells me to buy one. The table then applies "Ceiling" to synced storage and to a domain name, neither of which stops or resets; there it silently means "a predictable fixed price". Line 342 uses it for an upper bound on plausible spend, line 400 for a number of repetitions. By line 434 ("the ceiling is the one that cannot surprise you") I no longer knew which sense was active. The page notices this class of hazard elsewhere and warns about it (line 369), so it is clearly known.
findings.fix: Keep "ceiling" for Shape 1 only. Mark storage and domain in the Shape column as "Fixed" (or add a fourth shape: "a fixed fee — nothing to exhaust"). At line 342 use "upper bound"; at line 400 use "the cap is four rounds".

findings.title: "Token" is never defined, and an entire table is denominated in it
findings.where: First use line 323, "Per-token, on a card or a billing code"; then line 372 "Billable tokens", line 367 "$5 in / $25 out per million tokens", line 386 "read back out of cache"
findings.problem: I do not know what a token is. The page never tells me, and from line 323 onward it is the unit everything is priced in. "3,141,042" conveys nothing — I cannot tell whether that is a lot, whether it is the document or the reading of it, or why it is not simply the length of the file. "$5 in / $25 out" compounds it: nothing on the page says what goes in and what comes out, or why out costs five times in. "Cache" arrives at line 367 in the same condition, and "token consumption" closes the equity section at line 511. This is the section a cost-anxious reader most needs and the one that assumes the most.
findings.fix: Two sentences before the five-run table: "Agents are billed by the token — roughly three-quarters of a word, counted both on the way in (everything the agent reads) and on the way out (everything it writes). Writing costs about five times as much as reading, which is why the two rates differ." Then gloss "3.1 million tokens" once in human terms.

findings.title: "Active day" is an unexplained unit, and multiplying the two figures overshoots the range
findings.where: Line 338, "around $13 per developer per active day, and $150–250 per developer per month"
findings.problem: "Active day" is not defined — a day you touched it once, or a full working day? The first thing an anxious reader does with two numbers on one line is multiply: $13 × 20 working days = $260, above the top of the stated $150–250 range, and $13 × 30 = $390 is far above it. The figures reconcile only if you assume 11–19 active days a month, which the page never says. The reader's own arithmetic makes the page look wrong at the exact moment it is trying to reassure.
findings.fix: State the reconciling fact: "around $13 on a day they use it — and they use it 12 to 19 days a month, which is where the $150–250 comes from."

findings.title: The caption disclaims the word "Tier", which does not appear in that table
findings.where: Line 369, "“Tier” here means the model, not the plan — the plans in the table above are a different thing that unfortunately shares the word."
findings.problem: I hunted for "Tier" in the table headers and body and it is not there — the columns are Run, Billable tokens, At Opus‑5 rates, At Sonnet‑5 rates. A warning about a word I cannot find makes me assume I have missed a column, and it burns attention on a collision that no longer exists while the collision that does exist goes unhandled: nothing on this page says Opus‑5 and Sonnet‑5 are two sizes of model, or which is the "larger" one the caption's rates name. I had to infer that from column order. The same caption also fights itself — "the runs were not all on the same model, so the range is a band" (line 366) against "the two money columns are the same tokens priced at two different models" (line 368): if every row is repriced at one model per column, which model originally ran cannot matter.
findings.fix: Delete the "Tier" sentence (a leftover from an earlier header) and the "not all on the same model" clause, and spend the words on the mapping instead: "Opus‑5 and Sonnet‑5 are two sizes of the same vendor's model — the larger at $5/$25 per million, the mid-sized at $2/$10."

findings.title: The headline price is per round; the page then says a document takes up to four
findings.where: Line 384, "So: reviewing one document properly costs somewhere between $6 and $40." against line 400, "the ceiling for one document is four rounds — call it $64–160"
findings.problem: Both are stated as the cost of reviewing one document and they differ by a factor of four. The source settles which is right: OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1 records each of these measurements as "One round of eleven reviewers" and states "Cost is roles × rounds ... every round re-runs all eleven". So the five rows are five rounds and $6–$40 is one round, not one document. Line 388 then instructs me to carry the wrong number away — "That is the number worth carrying around" — and line 429's teaching estimate is built on it. A reader budgeting from this page underestimates the advertised unit by up to 4×. The page also never distinguishes "run" from "round": the caption says "Five complete eleven-agent runs", line 400 introduces "rounds" with no notice they are the same unit, so I could not tell whether four rounds meant four of the table's rows or something else again.
findings.fix: Use one word throughout — round — and state the unit at line 384: "So: one round of eleven readers costs $6 to $40, and a document usually takes two to four rounds — call it $12 to $160." Line 388's "number worth carrying around" should then be the per-document figure.

findings.title: "Fourteen rounds" directly contradicts the ceiling stated two sentences earlier
findings.where: Lines 399-403, "the ceiling for one document is four rounds ... One recorded run went fourteen rounds before a person stopped it."
findings.problem: I read "the ceiling ... is four rounds", took it as a hard limit — that is what ceiling has meant since line 264, where it is the thing that stops — and two sentences later the same paragraph reports fourteen. As written one of the two has to be false and a cold reader cannot tell which. The distinction the author holds (four is a configured cap; the fourteen-round run was not under it) is nowhere on the page. "Until it converges" is also unexplained, so I have no model of what ends a round. And the cost consequence is left unstated: fourteen rounds at these rates is roughly $224–560, which is the actual worst case this paragraph exists to warn about.
findings.fix: "The process repeats until the reviewers stop finding things. It is meant to stop at four rounds — call it $64–160 — but that limit is set by whoever runs it, and one recorded run went fourteen before a person noticed: somewhere north of $200."

findings.title: "Billable tokens" excludes tokens the same caption says are billed
findings.where: Line 372 header "Billable tokens"; line 363 "with cache reads charged at a tenth of the input rate"; line 385, "Between 10.8 and 36.9 million further tokens were read back out of cache on top of those figures"
findings.problem: Two problems in one place. A column labelled "Billable" that omits tokens the caption says are charged is a contradiction on its face — OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1 is explicit that cache reads are billed at a fraction and excluded from the billable count, and warns that "quoting either alone misleads". Worse for me as a reader: "on top of those figures" lands immediately after "reviewing one document properly costs somewhere between $6 and $40", so its nearest antecedent is the dollar range. I concluded the real bill was $6–$40 plus an unstated charge for 10.8–36.9 million more tokens. Whether the advertised price is the whole price is the single question this audience brings to the page.
findings.fix: Rename the column "Tokens read and written" (or "Counted tokens"), and make the antecedent explicit: "A further 10.8 to 36.9 million tokens were re-read from cache — already included in the dollar figures, at a tenth of the normal rate, and the reason the price does not simply track the length of the document."

findings.title: $5–15 a student appears with no derivation, and its input is withheld for two paragraphs
findings.where: Lines 422-423, "The university sizes its classroom allocation per user per month, for a term. One session is a fraction of a month, which puts it at an order of $5–15 a student"; the $50 it rests on appears only at line 443
findings.problem: "Which puts it at" performs a calculation I cannot see. I do not know the per-user monthly figure at this point — it is disclosed three paragraphs later, in a caveat box, as $50 from secondary coverage — so I cannot check $5–15, and I cannot tell whether "a fraction of a month" means a tenth or a third. This is the number a course convenor will actually take to a department head, so it is the one that most needs to be reproducible on sight. (The $30–90 for six students does check out: 6 × $5–15.)
findings.fix: Put the input in the sentence: "The university sizes its allocation per user per month — reported as $50, though its own page states no amount — and one 90-minute session is perhaps a tenth to a third of a month's use: an order of $5–15 a student, $30–90 for the room."

findings.title: Nine references to Cold Start sections, not one of them a link
findings.where: Lines 210 ("Cold Start 2.2"), 213 ("Cold Start Phase 7"), 217 ("Cold Start 1.3"), 477 ("Cold Start step 4.6"), 534 ("Cold Start 4.6.")
findings.problem: Every cross-reference is dead text. cold-start.html sits in the same folder and already carries matching anchors (id="2.2", id="1.3", id="4.6"), so each could be one click. As it stands the page's two most actionable instructions — "step 4.6 is where you go and look at your own numbers" and the final action item "Cold Start 4.6" — leave a reader who does not already have the other sheet open with nowhere to go. The reference style also shifts between bare numbers, "Phase 7" and "step 4.6", so I could not tell whether these were three different kinds of thing.
findings.fix: Link each one (cold-start.html#2.2 and so on) and settle on one label form — "Cold Start step 2.2" throughout, including for Phase 7.

findings.title: Five-run table hides the column that explains its own numbers
findings.where: Lines 371–381 (table head `<tr><th>Run</th><th>Billable tokens</th>…`) and line 384–386
findings.problem: The table invites the obvious arithmetic and then contradicts it: 17 Aug shows 1,786,769 tokens → $16, while 24 Aug shows fewer tokens (1,700,364) → nearly double the money ($30). A reader who trusts the table concludes the figures are wrong. The variable that resolves it — cache reads — is not in the table at all; it appears only as a range in the following paragraph ("Between 10.8 and 36.9 million further tokens were read back out of cache"). This is the page telling where it could show. It matters more than a normal ordering nit because cache reads are not a footnote: for the one run reconcilable against OPEN-CORRECTIONS C1 (28 Aug: 1,359,900 in / 236,512 out / 26,384,348 cache read), the arithmetic is 6.80 + 5.91 + 13.19 = $25.90 → the printed $26, of which 51% is cache reads. The majority of the headline price comes from a quantity the table does not print. The prose fix also introduces a misreading: "on top of those figures" sits directly under "$6 and $40", so it can be read as cache being an unbilled extra on top of the dollars, which would make the review cost roughly twice what the page says.
findings.fix: Add a fourth column, `Cache reads`, with the per-run figures (28 Aug is 26,384,348 from the C1 log; the others are the source of the 10.8–36.9M range already quoted). With that column present the non-proportionality is visible and the sentence at 384–386 shrinks to "cache reads are billed at a tenth of input, which is why dollars do not track billable tokens" — no ambiguous "on top of those figures" needed. If a five-column table is too wide for 600px, drop `At Sonnet-5 rates` to a single summary line and keep cache reads: the cache column does explanatory work the second money column does not.

findings.title: A 153-word caption carrying a rate card the columns should carry
findings.where: Lines 361–370, `<caption>Five complete eleven-agent runs…`
findings.problem: The caption is longer than the table it labels and holds five separable facts: provenance, computed-not-invoiced, model-not-plan, two full rate cards ($5 in / $25 out and $2 in / $10 out per million), and the cache discount. It is set at 12.5px in `var(--faint)` — the smallest, palest text on the page — and sits below a `min-width: 380px` overflow container, so on a phone it is the last thing reached and the hardest to read. It also says the same thing twice inside itself: line 363 "with cache reads charged at a tenth of the input rate" and lines 368–369 "with cached reading charged at a tenth of the input rate". Two of its clauses ("not two subscription plans", "'Tier' here means the model, not the plan") exist purely to defend against a misreading the column headers themselves create by naming models with no rates attached.
findings.fix: Put the rates in the headers, where they cannot be missed: `At Opus-5 — $5/$25 per Mtok` and `At Sonnet-5 — $2/$10 per Mtok`. That kills both defensive clauses and one of the duplicate cache sentences. Reduce the caption to two sentences: what was measured and when, and "computed from token counts at list rates, not read off an invoice."

findings.title: The plan-vs-meter comparison is a two-column table written as seven paragraphs
findings.where: Lines 417–439, "It is worth doing twice, because the two ways of sizing it disagree"
findings.problem: This section announces its own form — the same question costed two ways, and the gap between them is the argument. That is a comparison table by definition, and it is 404 words of prose with no visual break at all. The reader has to carry "$5–15 a student — $30–90 for the room" from one paragraph into the next to set it against "a few dollars in total for the whole room, not per student" — and the two are stated in different units (per student vs per room), so the comparison has to be reconstructed mentally before it can be felt. Worse, the size of the gap is never named. It is roughly 6× to 30× ($30–90 against ~$3–5 for the room), and "the gap between those two answers is not an error" lands far harder with a multiple attached than without one.
findings.fix: A four-row, two-column table: rows `Per student` / `For the room of six` / `What it is` / `What it protects you from`; columns `Priced as a plan (ceiling)` and `Priced as a meter`. Fill: $5–15 vs cents–low dollars; $30–90 vs a few dollars; "a ceiling you bought whether or not you reach it" vs "a bill for what you did"; "surprise in front of six students" vs "nothing". Add one line naming the multiple. The closing paragraphs at 431–439 then become the reading of the table rather than a substitute for it, and the section loses ~150 words.

findings.title: The equity section flattens an eligibility matrix that already exists as a table upstream
findings.where: Lines 479–511, esp. 487: "every student gets a chat box for free, and the agent sits behind an employment check and a departmental billing code"
findings.problem: 525 words, five h3s, one list, no table — the longest stretch on the page with no tabular structure, and the one carrying the most row-and-column-shaped facts. `points.md` §F holds these same facts as an actual four-row table (Service / Who / Cost / An agent?), and the page has dissolved it into a sentence. The loss is not decorative: the paragraph's own claim is that the institution "draws a line between chat and agent, and it draws it along employment status" — a line through a cohort is exactly the thing a matrix makes visible in one glance and a sentence makes the reader assemble. The $100 student-credit facts at line 491 (US/Canada only, .edu verification, works on a free account) are a fifth row of the same matrix, currently stranded under a separate h3 as if unrelated.
findings.fix: One generic table before or after "The institutional route is not evenly available": rows = chat tool / agent via institutional gateway / classroom provisioning / vendor student credits / personal card; columns = `Who can get it`, `Who pays`, `Is it an agent?`. Keep it institution-neutral, as the prose already is. Then fold the student-credit h3 into that table's last row and keep only its one-sentence sting ("it excludes them quietly, one at a time, at the point of sign-up") as prose. Everything else in this section — the free-tier-is-a-different-tool argument, the uncomfortable one at 511 — is moral reasoning, not structure, and should stay exactly as prose.

findings.title: The page's core cost mechanism gets one line of grey sub-text
findings.where: Line 461: "Your entire conversation is re-sent on every single request."
findings.problem: This is the single fact a non-programmer will not intuit, and it silently underwrites four other claims on the page: why cache reads dwarf billable tokens in the five-run table, why "start a fresh session" is "the largest lever you have", why eleven agents cost eleven times one, and why a loop left running overnight bills like work. It is currently 26 words of `var(--muted)` 13.5px sub-text inside a bullet — the lowest-emphasis typography on the page for the highest-leverage idea. Every other structural claim on this page has been given a container (three shapes, two tables, four lists); this one has not, and it is the only argument here whose shape is genuinely hard to convey in a sentence because it is cumulative and quadratic.
findings.fix: The one place a figure earns its place. A small inline SVG, ~5 bars: turn 1 sends 1 unit, turn 2 sends 2, turn 3 sends 3, turn 5 sends 5 — with a caption giving the cumulative total (15 units of billing for 5 questions), and a second short bar beside it showing the same 5 questions asked in fresh sessions (5 units). Two bar groups, no axes needed. Alternatively, if no figure is wanted, promote the sentence out of the bullet into a `.note` box before the list, since the whole list depends on it.

findings.title: An explicitly ranked list rendered as an unranked one, with no magnitudes
findings.where: Line 456: "Four things move it, in roughly this order" followed by `<ul class="plain">` at 458
findings.problem: The sentence makes an ordering claim and the markup discards it: `ul.plain` renders four visually identical, unnumbered rows, so nothing on screen distinguishes the largest lever from the smallest. The ranking survives only as a buried adjective in the first item's sub-text ("the largest lever you have"). The page has the right component for this already — `ol.acts` at line 168 draws visible accent-coloured numerals — and it is spent on "What to do", a list whose items are far less order-dependent. The two are backwards. Compounding it, three of the four levers have knowable magnitudes and none is given: model choice is "several times" (the caption's own rate cards make that $5/$25 vs $2/$10, i.e. 2.5×), agent count is linear in N, and vagueness is the difference between reading everything and reading two files.
findings.fix: Switch this list to `ol.acts` so the ranking is visible, and attach a magnitude to each item's sub-text where one exists — "2.5× between the largest and mid-sized model", "×N, and N is however many you launched". The order claim then does not need the words "in roughly this order" at all.

findings.title: 187-word provenance paragraph: seven discrete sources, no structure, smallest type
findings.where: Line 541, the third `<footer>` paragraph, "The five-run worked example is derived from a token log…"
findings.problem: This is the densest block on the page and the least readable: 187 unbroken words at 12.5px in `var(--faint)`, containing seven separately-sourced claims (the token log, vendor prices, Anthropic's cost docs, the institutional check, the student-credit check, the teaching estimates, the link check) each with its own date and confidence level — including two genuinely load-bearing warnings that the log "is not yet published" and that the $50 figure is secondary-coverage-only. Provenance is a table of what / from where / when / how solid, and burying it as a run-on paragraph makes the two warnings indistinguishable from the routine dates around them. It also repeats material already stated in stronger positions upstream: the model-not-plan clarification (already twice in the caption at 366 and 369), the $50 caveat (already in the flag at 443), and "29 August 2026", which appears seven times across the page.
findings.fix: Convert to `ul.plain`, one row per source, with the source in `<b>` and date plus confidence in `.sub` — the component is already defined and styled. Drop the model-not-plan sentence entirely once the rate cards move into the table headers (see the caption finding), and drop the $50 restatement since the flag box at 441–452 says it with more force. That is ~60 words removed and the two real warnings become the two rows a reader's eye can land on.

findings.title: Shape column collapses three shapes back into two; Shape 3 never appears
findings.where: Lines 294–331, the `<th>Shape</th>` column, and line 323 "Per-token, on a card or a billing code"
findings.problem: The three-shape taxonomy is the page's best structural idea and the pricing table is where it should pay off — but the column reads Ceiling six times and Meter once, so it carries almost no information as printed, and the row that should carry Shape 3 merges it with Shape 2 under a single "Meter". Shape 3 is the one with the worst named failure mode ("a conversation with your head of department about a number") and the one most relevant to the faculty readers deciding whether to assign this, and it is the only shape absent from the table that is supposed to apply the taxonomy.
findings.fix: Split line 323 into two rows — "Per-token, on your own card" (Shape 2) and "Per-token, on an institutional billing code" (Shape 3) — and label the column cells `Shape 1`/`Shape 2`/`Shape 3` rather than the words, so the table reads as an index back into the grid above it. Both new rows keep "whatever you use"; what differs is who receives the bill, which is the whole point of separating them.

findings.title: No print styles: dark-theme tokens survive onto paper
findings.where: Line 52 `:root[data-theme="dark"] {` and line 55 `--ink:     #E3E8EE;`; `grep -n '@media print' what-it-costs.html` returns nothing
findings.problem: FAIL. The file has no `@media print` block — verified by grep, and by contrast `four-barriers.html` in the same directory has one. Two consequences. First and airtight: the dark palette at lines 52–67 is applied by a bare attribute selector with no media guard, so when a reader has explicitly chosen the dark theme (the artifact host stamps `data-theme="dark"` on the root), those tokens are still in force at print time in every browser. Printing then strips `body { background: var(--ground) }` — browsers drop backgrounds by default — but keeps `color: var(--ink)`, which is `#E3E8EE`. That is a near-white grey on white paper. The page is the money sheet; the numbers, the three shapes, the equity section all come out blank. Second, and browser-specific: Chromium and WebKit evaluate `prefers-color-scheme` against the OS setting during print, so the block at lines 33–50 fires the same way for a system-dark reader who never touched the toggle. Beyond colour, nothing controls pagination — the two `.tw` tables, the three `.shape` cards and the `.flag` blocks can all be split across a page break, and the outbound URLs (claude.com/pricing, the murderboard repo, the costs docs) vanish entirely on paper, which is exactly the material the staleness banner at line 224 tells the reader to go and check.
findings.fix: Add a print block before the `@media (max-width: 460px)` rule at line 188: `@media print { :root, :root[data-theme="dark"] { --ground:#fff; --surface:#fff; --sunk:#F2F5F8; --ink:#171C23; --muted:#444; --faint:#555; --rule:#CCC; --rule-firm:#999; --accent:#15577D; --accent-soft:#fff; --caution:#8A5D0F; --caution-soft:#fff; --good:#2E6A4F; } body { padding:0; font-size:11pt; } .page { max-width:none; } .tw, table, .shape, .flag, .note, .stale, ul.plain > li, ol.acts > li { break-inside: avoid; } h2, h3 { break-after: avoid; } .tw { overflow-x: visible; } table { min-width:0; } a[href^="http"]::after { content:" (" attr(href) ")"; font-size:9pt; color:#555; word-break:break-all; } }` The re-declaration of `:root[data-theme="dark"]` inside the print block is the load-bearing part — without it the attribute selector wins.

findings.title: Heading level skipped: h2 jumps straight to h4
findings.where:
Lines 265, 271, 277 — `

A subscription

`, `

Pay per use, on your own card

`, `

An institutional billing code

`
findings.problem: FAIL on heading hierarchy. The document order is h1 (197) → h2 (229, 235, 258) → h4 (265, 271, 277), with no h3 anywhere before them; the first h3 does not appear until line 336. Level 3 is skipped, which breaks the document outline and heading-based navigation for anyone using a screen reader — the three card titles announce as level 4 nested directly under level 2. The visual hierarchy is inverted on top of that: `.shape h4` is 15px bold ink (line 141) while `h3` is 11px uppercase mono accent (lines 100–103), so the element that claims the deeper level is the more prominent one. These are card titles inside `.shape` divs, not a subordinate section of the h2 above them.
findings.fix:
Either promote them to `h3` and change the selector at line 141 from `.shape h4` to `.shape h3` (the existing `h3` rule at 100–103 would need `.shape h3 { font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 15px; text-transform: none; letter-spacing: 0; color: var(--ink); font-weight: 600; margin: 0 0 6px; }` to keep the card look), or — simpler and truer to what they are — demote them to `

` with the same styling, since a card title inside a three-card grid is not a section heading at all.

findings.title: Long provenance caption trapped in a horizontal scroller
findings.where: Lines 359–370: `<div class="tw">` … `<caption>Five complete eleven-agent runs across three projects…` (a ~750-character block), with `.tw { overflow-x: auto }` at line 147 and `min-width: 380px` at line 148
findings.problem: The `<caption>` is part of the table box, so it inherits the table's `min-width: 380px` and is laid out inside the `overflow-x: auto` scroller. On a 360px phone the body padding drops to 14px each side (line 189), leaving ~332px of content width against a 380px table, so roughly 48px — about six characters — is cut off the right edge of every line of that caption, and the reader has to scroll horizontally to read a 750-character methodology paragraph. The same applies to the shorter caption at line 292. This is the paragraph that carries the whole honesty case for the money figures — that they are computed rather than invoiced, that the two columns are models and not plans — and it is the one non-tabular element on the page put behind a horizontal scroll for no reason.
findings.fix:
Move both caption blocks out of the tables and render them as siblings after the `.tw` div: `

…

` with `.src { font-size: 12.5px; color: var(--faint); margin: 8px 0 0; }`, which reproduces the current `caption` styling at lines 157–160. The tables lose nothing — `caption-side: bottom` was already putting them below — and the prose then wraps to the viewport.

findings.title: Table 1's caption names four sources; one row comes from none of them
findings.where: Line 292 caption: "Read 29 August 2026 from the vendors' own pages — Claude, Codex, Gemini CLI, Dropbox" against line 328 row: "A domain name — only if you want one"
findings.problem: The caption enumerates the sources for the table exhaustively — four named vendors. The last row prices a domain name at ~$10–15/yr, which comes from a registrar and is not attributable to Claude, Codex, Gemini CLI or Dropbox. A caption that lists its sources by name and then omits one is a small hole in exactly the provenance discipline the rest of the page is built on, and it is the row a reader is most likely to want to check because the bullet at line 213 warns them the renewal price is the number that matters. (The Dropbox row at 318 is also the only row with no link, though the caption does name Dropbox as a source.)
findings.fix: Either extend the caption to "…Claude, Codex, Gemini CLI, Dropbox, and one registrar's published renewal prices", or add an inline link on the domain row the way the Gemini CLI, ChatGPT Go and Claude Pro rows already carry one.

findings.title: Dead custom property declared three times, never used
findings.where: Line 27 `--good-soft: #E6F1EB;`, line 48 `--good-soft: #14261E;`, line 66 `--good-soft: #14261E;`
findings.problem: `--good-soft` is defined in all three token blocks — light, prefers-dark, and `[data-theme="dark"]` — and `grep` for `var(--good-soft)` across the file returns nothing. All 15 other tokens are used. It is carried over from a sibling sheet in the same system and now costs three lines of maintenance every time the palette is touched, with the standing risk that a future edit updates two of the three and nobody notices because nothing renders it.
findings.fix: Delete lines 27, 48 and 66. If the intent was to give the `.shape` cards (which use `--good` at line 138) a tinted background to match the `.shape.meter` treatment, use it — otherwise it should go.

findings.title: The page's own nominated takeaway sits at 60% depth
findings.where: Line 388: "That is the number worth carrying around, because it is the shape of every real task"
findings.problem: The page explicitly labels one sentence as the thing to carry away — "a few dollars for a serious piece of work, and a few cents for a small one" (lines 389-390) — and places it after five other sections, including the largest and most alarming number on the sheet ($13/day, $150-250/month, line 338) and a table of million-token counts. A frightened reader's first question is the order of magnitude of ordinary use. The standfirst (line 198) promises "what a working setup actually costs"; the plan prices arrive at the table (line 308), but the per-task magnitude — the one that converts fear into a working mental model — does not arrive until roughly 60% down. Readers who bail early leave with $150-250/month as their anchor.
findings.fix: Put the magnitude into the opening. At line 222, after "You can complete every step of Cold Start without paying anyone", add one clause: "and when you do pay, ordinary work runs to cents for a small task and single dollars for a serious one — the rest of this page is where those figures come from." Leave the worked example exactly where it is; it then reads as evidence for a claim already made rather than a late reveal.

findings.title: The danger and its five-minute fix are 250 lines apart
findings.where: Line 272: "Most such accounts can be given a spend limit. Almost nobody sets one." vs line 526
findings.problem: Shape 2 diagnoses the page's worst outcome and withholds the instruction. The instruction — "If it is a meter, set the spend limit the same day you set up the account" — is item 4 of 5 in the closing list at line 525, and the page itself says at line 526 that this "stops the only genuinely bad outcome on this page." A reader who is currently on a meter, currently anxious, reads the diagnosis at line 272 and must survive nine screens of prices, token tables and equity argument before being told what to do about it. This is the one place on the page where reading order maps onto real financial exposure.
findings.fix: Make the imperative land inside the Shape 2 card. Replace "Almost nobody sets one" with "Almost nobody sets one. Set yours today, before the first real session — it is a five-minute job and it is the only thing on this page that prevents a bill you did not agree to." Keep the item in the closing list as the reminder; the closing list is where it belongs as a checklist, not where it belongs as a first warning.

findings.title: The closing action list drops the instructor, one of the two audiences
findings.where: Lines 515-536, "What to do" — all five items
findings.problem: Every one of the five closing actions addresses an individual buying for themselves: "your own money", "your own account", "who reads the statement", "your own usage." But the page spends two full sections on the teaching case (line 415, "What one teaching session costs") and an entire h2 on what you owe students (line 493, "If you are teaching, you are assigning an expense"). The instructor's actions exist only at lines 496-507, mid-page, inside the equity argument. A reader who came to this page to decide whether to assign it to students reaches the end and finds nothing addressed to them — the takeaway list silently reverts to the single-user frame the page had already outgrown.
findings.fix: Add a sixth item to the ol.acts: "If you are assigning this to other people, cost one real session before you assign it" with a sub carrying the two rules that already exist at lines 501-507 in compressed form — provision centrally if you can, and do not let the free tier be the contingency for whoever could not pay. It is three lines and it closes the loop the equity section opens.

findings.title: Opening list gives its detail to the costs that do not matter
findings.where: Lines 203-220, and specifically line 206: "This is the whole of the rest of this page, because it is the only one where the amount is open-ended."
findings.problem: The list's weights are inverted against the reader's fear. Item 1 (the agent) is the only open-ended cost and the reason anyone opened the page, and it gets one clause plus a deferral. Items 2-4 are bounded, small, or — by the page's own admission at line 217 — needed by almost nobody, and they get the prose. Item 2's sub (line 210) is the longest block in the list and detours into Cold Start 2.3's sync-reliability rule. So the first substantive paragraph on a page titled "What It Costs", for a reader anxious about agent bills, is about Dropbox's 2 GB tier. The deferral is defensible as structure; the imbalance in front of it is not.
findings.fix: Give item 1 a magnitude so the deferral is a promise rather than a withholding: "free tiers exist and are real, but they are the part you outgrow first — for almost everyone the answer turns out to be $0-20 a month." Then cut item 2's sub to its first sentence plus the paid price, and drop the 2.3 cross-reference to a parenthetical; the reliability rationale is Cold Start's job, not this page's.

findings.title: The loudest block on the page arrives 60 lines before the figures it governs
findings.where: Line 109 CSS comment "staleness banner: the loudest thing on the page"; banner at lines 224-227; the table it is about at lines 290-334
findings.problem: The banner is the first bordered, coloured block a reader hits, and it is deliberately the loudest thing on the sheet. Its content is meta — these numbers rot — not decision-relevant. For an anxious reader arriving in paragraph three, the strongest visual signal on the page currently says "nothing here can be trusted", before any of the page's credibility has been built and 60 lines before the table it actually governs. The h2 at line 288 is already titled "Numbers, with all the caveats attached", which is precisely where a caveat about numbers belongs.
findings.fix: Move the .stale block to sit immediately under the h2 at line 288, heading the section whose figures it qualifies. Keep one short sentence in its current position if the early warning is wanted — "Every figure here was read on 29 August 2026; treat them as orders of magnitude" — as plain text rather than the page's loudest block. The staleness argument does not weaken by being adjacent to the numbers; it gets stronger.
